It computes four component rasters — slope suitability (based on degree thresholds: 0–15°=100, >35°=0), view orientation suitability (based on aspect direction with preferential scoring for south/southwest for sea/sunset views), access distance suitability (distance from roads or parcel centroid, scored 100 at 0–20 m down to 10 beyond 100 m), and drainage safety suitability (using flow accumulation statistics or inverse slope as proxy). These are combined using fixed or configurable weights (40% slope, 20% each for view, access, drainage) into a final suitability raster. Outputs include five georeferenced GeoTIFFs: slope_suitability.tif, view_suitability.tif, access_suitability.tif, drainage_suitability.tif, and suitability_combined.tif — plus statistical validation (mean, histogram by class, validation checks) and human-readable interpretation of site quality (e.g., 'Excellent overall site quality' if mean ≥ 80).

The script extracts a binary surface water mask from a pre-downloaded satellite image raster by thresholding the blue band (band 3) between DN values 75–100. It applies NoData masking, gap-filling via interpolation, re-binarization (≥0.5 → 1), sieving to remove small noisy regions (<500 pixels), and polygonization—retaining only polygons with DN=1 to guarantee water-only vector output. Final outputs include a cleaned 0/1 raster mask and a GeoPackage of water body polygons.

The script identifies contiguous raster cells with population ≥300 per cell, groups them into spatially connected clusters (using GRASS r.clump), filters clusters whose total population sum ≥5000, clips and smooths the resulting cluster raster using a majority filter (5-of-8 neighborhood rule) to fill nodata gaps and reduce noise, then converts the smoothed cluster raster into vector polygons. The final output is a shapefile (HighDensityClusters.shp) where each polygon represents a statistically and spatially coherent high-density urban cluster derived from gridded population data.

task_name: Generate topographic surface from contour lines
task_description: The script converts a vector layer of contour lines ('Horizontals.shp') into a raster digital elevation model (DEM) via TIN interpolation; computes its basic statistics (min/mean/max); adds a constant offset (+4842) to the DEM; then derives aspect and slope rasters, followed by reclassification of slope into five ordinal classes (0–10°→1, ..., 41–50°→5). Outputs include: Horizontals_Tin.tif (interpolated DEM), Horizontals_Tin_Calc.tif (offset DEM), ASP.tif (aspect), SLP.tif (slope), and Rec_SLP.tif (reclassified slope).

task_name: Download and mosaic OPR DEM tiles
task_description: The script downloads USGS 3DEP Original Project Raster (OPR) Digital Elevation Model (DEM) tiles that spatially intersect a user-provided Area of Interest (AOI) polygon, filters them by ground sample distance (GSD) to prioritize highest-resolution tiles, creates a seamless GDAL-based mosaic (VRT + warp), optionally clips the mosaic to the AOI bounds, converts elevation values from meters to feet, and optionally generates contour lines at a specified interval in DXF, Shapefile, or GeoPackage format — all saved to a user-specified output folder with a manifest CSV listing downloaded tiles and metadata.

The script performs plate-by-plate TIN interpolation of elevation-like node points (water-load-corrected) in a global equal-area projection (ESRI:54034), followed by nodata filling and polygon clipping per tectonic plate, ultimately generating a mosaic of plate-clipped rasters to produce a final filled global elevation raster for a given geological age. Inputs include precomputed point layers ('all_nodes_*.geojson') tagged with plate names (e.g., 'Nazca', 'India') and appearance age, and plate polygon layers ('Plate Polygons') filtered by age. The workflow includes longitude clamping, reprojection using CEA (Cylindrical Equal Area), buffering to refine plate boundaries, spatial filtering of nodes by plate identity and intersection, per-plate interpolation, clipping to refined plate polygons, and mosaicking.

task_name: Generate SWAT HRUs from landuse soil slope rasters
task_description: The script generates Hydrologic Response Units (HRUs) for the SWAT hydrological model by spatially intersecting and aggregating landuse, soil, and slope raster grids with watershed subbasin and channel delineation data. It supports multiple HRU generation strategies (dominant HRU, dominant landuse/soil/slope, or threshold-based filtering by area/percentage of landuse, soil, or slope classes), incorporates landscape units (floodplain/upslope), handles reservoir/pond identification and merging, produces shapefiles (FullHRUs, actual HRUs, LSUs), writes HRU metadata to a SQLite database (gis_hrus, gis_subbasins, gis_lsus, gis_water), and generates comprehensive text reports (topographic, basin, HRU).

task_name: Simplify flight waypoints using DEM-constrained 3D tolerance
task_description: The script simplifies a drone flight plan (input CSV with longitude, latitude, and altitude(m)) by: (1) converting points to a 3D vector layer in WGS84; (2) sampling elevation values from a user-provided DEM raster; (3) reprojecting to a user-specified projected CRS; (4) constructing the original trajectory line ordered by 'original_index'; (5) simplifying that line using Douglas-Peucker (tolerance parameter); (6) extracting vertices of the simplified line; (7) buffering those vertices; (8) spatially joining original reprojected points to buffers to identify which original waypoints fall within tolerance envelopes; and (9) filtering the input CSV to retain only those rows whose line index matches the retained waypoints — producing a reduced, terrain-aware, Litchi-compatible CSV output. Optional outputs include original CSV points, simplified trajectory line (with arrow styling), and simplified CSV points layers added to QGIS project.

The script processes high-resolution eReefs hydrodynamic model grid shapefiles to derive simplified, buffered boundary polygons for spatial containment checks. It first dissolves grid cells where depth > 0 to extract the model domain boundary, then applies a buffer (in degrees) followed by geometry simplification (tolerance = 2 × buffer distance) to create a low-detail version suitable for fast point-in-polygon queries—intentionally over-inclusive to avoid false negatives during inverse distance weighted interpolation of model outputs. Outputs include: (1) dissolved high-res boundary shapefiles (.shp and .geojson), (2) buffered intermediate shapefiles, and (3) simplified low-detail boundaries in GeoJSON format with filenames suffixed '_ld-boundary.geojson'.

The script builds a cartographic elevation diagram for Brazilian Army topographic mapping. It processes elevation point data (elemnat_ponto_cotado_p), generalizes them based on map scale, generates terrain slicing rasters (elevation classes) and contour layers from a digital elevation model (MDE), integrates hydrography (cobter_massa_dagua_a, elemnat_trecho_drenagem_l), infrastructure (infra_vala_l), and area-without-data masks (llp_area_sem_dados_a), applies QGIS layer styles from local QML files, configures layout grids with custom annotation expressions aligned to SIRGAS/4674 CRS, inserts SVG-based color bars scaled to class count (2–4 classes), and optionally generalizes drainage networks using geometric constraints. Outputs include styled raster/vector layers added to the QGIS project, updated print layout items (map extent, grids, scale bar, class labels), and a grouped layer tree node for visualization control.

The script calculates the Morphological Quality Index (IQM9) for river segments using nine individual indices (A1–A4, F1–F5) derived from geospatial inputs. It processes a segmented stream network (CRHQ UEA), computes watershed delineation using a LiDAR DEM and D8 flow direction, integrates anthropogenic features (dams, roads, structures), land use, riparian forest bands, and channel width measurements from PtRef points. Each index quantifies a specific morphological stressor (e.g., A1: upstream watershed area ratio; A3: dam proximity; F2/F3: road encroachment in floodplain; F5: riparian forest continuity). Final IQM is computed per segment as '1 - (sum of nine indices)/40', outputting a line vector layer with attribute fields for each index and the composite 'Score IQM9'.

The script computes the closest point on a line feature to each input point, returning a table with five columns: input_id, input_lat, input_lon, line_lat, line_lon. It achieves this through a multi-step workflow: (1) fixing geometries and converting multipart to singlepart; (2) adding XY coordinates to points; (3) using GRASS v.distance to generate shortest-distance line segments; (4) joining attributes and extracting vertices from those segments; (5) filtering for the vertex on the target line (using 'distance > 0' condition); and (6) copying and renaming coordinate fields to produce the final output with standardized field names. The method find_closest_coordinates_from_points_to_lines encapsulates this entire workflow and returns a vector layer with the computed coordinates.

The script extracts sub-watersheds from a segmented stream network (CRHQ) using D8 flow direction rasters, assigns segment IDs to each sub-watershed polygon, computes total watershed area, reclassifies MELCCFP land use raster into four classes (forest, agricultural, anthropogenic, aquatic), calculates area (m²) of each land use class per sub-watershed via zonal histogram and pixel-area scaling (100 m² per 10×10 m pixel), optionally aggregates dam drainage areas (from CEHQ dam points) per sub-watershed using D8-based basin delineation and spatial join summation, and outputs a vector layer of sub-watershed polygons with attributes: segment ID, total watershed area, forest_area, agri_area, anthro_area, water_area, land_area, and dam_area_sum.

The script burns vector-based drainage networks into a digital elevation model (DEM) by rasterizing the drainage layers, converting both DEM and drainage to PCRaster format, preparing a boolean drainage mask using cover, and applying a custom 'burndem' algorithm that creates a smooth drop over a user-defined buffer distance and an additional sharp drop directly at the drainage line. The output is a modified DEM raster where elevation values are lowered along and near drainage features to enforce hydrological connectivity.

task_name: Derive watershed basin from DEM and discharge point
task_description: The script computes the upslope drainage basin for a user-specified discharge point using a filled DEM and SAGA GIS 'upslopearea' algorithm. It then converts the resulting raster basin to vector (polygonized), fixes geometries, dissolves features, filters to retain only the target watershed, clips the DEM to that basin, generates contour lines at 100 m intervals, clips the input channel network to the basin boundary, and computes watershed-level statistics and Curve Numbers (CN) by intersecting with soil and Corine land cover layers. Outputs include: (1) raw and filtered basin polygons (GPKG), (2) clipped basin DEM (GeoTIFF), (3) 100-m contour lines (GPKG), (4) basin-restricted channel network (GPKG), (5) CN-weighted polygon layer (GPKG), and (6) Corine and SCS land use classification layers (GPKG).

The script computes a kernel density estimation (KDE) heatmap from an input point vector layer using QGIS's native 'qgis:heatmapkerneldensityestimation' algorithm, then applies a pseudocolor raster style (including color ramp selection, inversion, interpolation mode, classification mode, and number of gradient classes) via the custom 'densityanalysis:rasterstyle' algorithm. Outputs include a styled raster density map with user-configurable pixel size, kernel radius (converted to CRS units), kernel shape, decay (for triangular), output scaling, and styling parameters. All parameters are exposed as QGIS Processing inputs with validation and feedback reporting.

The script extracts outlet points from a segmented stream network by interpolating points near the downstream ends of each line segment (using a dynamic distance based on segment length), rasterizes the stream network using a LiDAR-derived 10 m DEM, snaps the interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within 40 m using WhiteboxTools' JensonSnapPourPoints, and joins the original segment ID attribute (e.g., 'Id_UEA') from the stream network to the snapped points via nearest-neighbor join (max distance 50 m). The output is a point vector layer where each feature represents a snapped outlet with its associated segment identifier.

task_name: Convert GWSW sewer network to GeoDyn input
task_description: The script converts a municipal sewer network dataset (GWSW) into GeoDyn-compatible input layers for hydrodynamic modeling. It processes vector layers representing bemalingsgebieden (catchments), netwerk_knooppunt (nodes), netwerk_kunstwerk (structures like pumps, overflows, and culverts), and netwerk_verbinding (pipes). Key steps include: (1) extracting and filtering structures by type (e.g., 'Pomp', 'Doorlaatniveau', 'Overstortdrempel'); (2) spatially joining pipes to catchments using 'within' and 'nearest' relationships; (3) generating BEM_ID and STELSEL_ID identifiers; (4) computing storage volumes in pipes ('Berging_leiding_parts') and nodes ('BergingInKnopen') based on geometry, pipe/structure dimensions, and elevation data (e.g., 'Maaiveldhoogte', 'Drempelniveau', 'BobBeginpuntLeiding'); (5) aggregating per-catchment statistics (counts of pumps, overflows, culverts; total storage in m³); and (6) producing standardized output layers including 'Gebiedsgegevens_punt_tbv_stap2' (point features with attributes like BERGING_M3, POMPEN_ST, OVERSTORT_, DOORLAAT_S) and 'Gebiedsgegevens_lijn_tbv_stap2' (line features joined with storage values). All outputs are structured for direct ingestion into the GeoDyn modeling suite.

The script performs spatial interpolation of a user-specified numeric field (e.g., soil nutrient concentration, pH, or moisture) from point vector data to generate a continuous raster surface. It supports four methods: Thiessen (nearest-neighbor tessellation), Voronoi (geometric partitioning), Delaunay triangulation (with attribute joining), and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) via GRASS v.surf.idw. For tessellation methods, it first creates polygons (Thiessen/Voronoi/Delaunay), clips them to the convex hull of input points, then rasterizes the resulting vector layer using the specified field and pixel resolution. For IDW, it directly invokes GRASS IDW interpolation. Outputs are a single GeoTIFF raster at user-defined grid resolution (meters).

The script performs spatial sampling of a user-provided raster layer by generating point features at pixel centers and selecting a user-defined number of points either randomly (unstratified) or stratified by reclassifying the raster into quantiles, equal intervals, or K-means classes. For stratified sampling, it first applies a custom classification algorithm ('Precision Agriculture:R - Classification'), converts the classified raster to points, filters out 'nan' values, then performs random selection within each class subset. The final output is a vector layer of sampling points with added X/Y coordinate fields.

The script computes the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) erosion potential raster using a filled-sinks DEM and optional or single-value K, C, and R factor inputs. It first calculates the LS factor using the 'LS Mitasova' algorithm (which derives slope, flow accumulation, and LS from the DEM with user-defined sheet and rill erosion factors), then constructs a dynamic raster algebra expression (e.g., 'A*B*C*D' or substituted numeric values) combining LS, K, C, and R components via GDAL's raster calculator. Outputs are two rasters: the intermediate LS Area raster (slope-length factor) and the final RUSLE raster (predicted soil loss in tons/ha/year).

The script delineates a stream network and its corresponding catchment boundary from a user-specified outlet point and study extent. It downloads a DEM from OpenTopography (e.g., SRTM or Copernicus), reprojects it, converts it to PCRaster format, computes flow direction using lddcreate, derives Strahler-order streams, snaps the outlet to the nearest stream within a tolerance, calculates the catchment raster via catchment(), and outputs vectorized streams (as line features) and a polygonized catchment boundary (as a single-polygon feature). Intermediate rasters (DEM, flow direction, river, outlet buffer, snapped outlet, catchment) are written to a user-specified folder in PCRaster .map format.

The script generates Voronoi tessellations from input point features (e.g., random points inside polygons or centroids of k-means clusters) using QGIS processing algorithms. It supports two main workflows: (1) splitting a polygon layer into Voronoi-derived subregions via random point generation, k-means clustering, centroid extraction, buffering, and intersection; and (2) computing Voronoi-based medial axes/skeletons for linear features. Outputs are vector layers — either intersected Voronoi polygons clipped to input boundaries or simplified, dissolved, directional-merged skeleton lines.

The script processes a user-provided sub-basin polygon layer to compute: (1) maximum and minimum elevation per sub-basin using a DEM via zonal statistics; (2) sub-basin area in hectares; (3) mean imperviousness per sub-basin, either by raster zonal statistics (if imperviousness layer is raster) or by vector intersection + weighted area aggregation (if imperviousness layer is vector); (4) longest flow path (LFP) per sub-basin using WhiteboxTools' LongestFlowpath algorithm on a burn-and-fill preprocessed DEM clipped per sub-basin; (5) LFP rotation (flow direction) relative to south; (6) ZOUT point (outlet) derived as the intersection of the lowest-elevation border sub-basin with the outer boundary of the full sub-basin set. Outputs include: a processed GeoPackage layer with all computed attributes; a GPKG LFP layer; optional SQLite database export conforming to QTalsim schema (with SystemElement and SubBasin tables, WGS84-transformed geometries, and scenario metadata); and optional ASCII-formatted EZG file for Talsim NG4 with fixed-field layout based on a template.

The script executes a multi-phase bathymetric inversion pipeline for Satellite-Derived Bathymetry (SDB) using optical satellite imagery. It performs pre-processing (Phase 1: band selection, sun glint correction, water masking, feature stack generation), point-based filtering (Phase 2: RANSAC outlier removal on training points), global modeling (Phase 3: ensemble ML regression—Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Extra Trees, SVR, MLP—to predict depth from spectral features), optional adaptive refinement (Phase 4: localized model retraining using additional adaptive training points), and post-processing (clamping to max_depth, removing positive-depth pixels, slope-based depth filtering). Outputs include Phase 3 initial depth map, Phase 4 refined depth map, clipped feature stacks, water masks, cleaned/filtered rasters, and validation reports if enabled.

The script resamples Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) vegetation biophysical variables (e.g., NDVI, LAI, FAPAR) from 333m to 1km resolution while preserving the original 1km spatial extent and time-series compatibility. It applies a two-path resampling workflow: (1) 'average' resampling of the input raster with scaling and offset correction, and (2) 'mode' resampling of a reclassified version (using user-defined class boundaries); then multiplies the two outputs and applies a final integer conversion formula incorporating user-specified offset (-0.08) and scaling (250) to produce a UInt32 compressed GeoTIFF output. The resampling bounds are fixed to global terrestrial extent: X ∈ [-179.995536, 179.995536], Y ∈ [-59.995536, 79.995536], matching the CGLS 1km grid (1/112° ≈ 0.00893°).

The script calculates terrain slope from a user-provided DEM raster using GDAL's slope algorithm. It first checks if the input DEM is in a geographic CRS; if so, it reprojects it to a user-specified projected CRS using gdal:warpreproject (bilinear resampling). Then it computes slope either in percentage (%) for FAO, USDA/NRCS, or Embrapa thematic styles, or in degrees (°) for CAR/Brazilian Forest Code style. The output is a classified slope raster with appropriate units and optional thematic styling applied via 'lftools:magicstyles'. A post-processor renames the output layer according to the selected style.

The script resamples Copernicus Global Land Cover (CGLS) 333m raster products to 1km resolution while preserving the spatial extent of legacy 1km time series. It first reclassifies input raster values using a user-defined table (e.g., mapping [-0.08,0.92,1,0.92,255,0] to recode invalid pixels), then performs two parallel GDAL translate operations: one with 'average' resampling (for continuous variables like NDVI/FAPAR/LAI) and one with 'mode' resampling (for categorical land cover), followed by a raster calculator multiplying the two outputs, and finally compresses and exports the result as a GeoTIFF. The workflow is explicitly tuned for Copernicus vegetation biophysical variables (NDVI, FAPAR, LAI) and references CGLS PROBA-V and Sentinel-3 origins.

The script extracts outlet points along a stream network by interpolating points near the downstream ends of stream lines (using a dynamic distance based on line length), rasterizes the stream network using a DEM as base, and then snaps the interpolated points to the nearest stream pixel within a 40-unit distance using the Jenson Snap Pour Points algorithm. The output is a vector point layer of snapped outlets.

task_name: Compute Integrated Quality Index for rivers
task_description: The script computes an Integrated Quality Index (IQM) for river networks by aggregating nine standardized indices (A1–A4, F1–F5) derived from hydrographic, topographic, land use, infrastructure, and riparian zone data. It begins by computing a D8 flow direction raster from a DEM and stream network, filters point structures near rivers/roads, then sequentially calculates A1–A3 and F1 using dams, land use, reference points (width measurements), streams, and filtered structures; followed by A4 (likely channel gradient or confinement), F2–F5 (anthropogenic pressure indices involving roads, land use, width ratios, and riparian buffer integrity). Finally, it computes the final IQM score as '1 - (sum of all 9 indices)/38' and appends it as a 'Score IQM' field to the output vector layer representing the river network.

The script generates hydrological drainage relationships between catchment areas (bemalingsgebieden) using vector network analysis. It computes point-on-surface centroids for catchments, extracts start/end vertices of drainage lines (leidingen), joins these vertices to catchments via spatial intersection to assign 'VAN_BEM_ID' and 'NAAR_BEM_ID', constructs a 'VAN_NAAR' string identifier, filters out self-loops (VAN == NAAR), sorts and deduplicates by VAN_NAAR while prioritizing higher BERGING_M3 and shorter length, selects corresponding drainage lines, builds an afvoerboom (drainage tree) using hub-lines from downstream to upstream catchment centroids, aggregates storage volume (BERGING_M3) per BEM_ID from point data, joins storage and topology attributes to catchment polygons, and outputs five key layers: (1) catchments with drainage relations (Bemalingsgebieden_met_afvoerrelaties_tbv_stap3), (2) deduplicated directed edge table (VAN_NAAR_SEL), (3) selected drainage lines (Gebiedsgegevens_lijn_selectie), (4) end points within terminal catchments (eindpunten_in_eindgebied_selected), and (5) the drainage tree as line features (afvoerboom). All operations are purely vector-based and rely on QGIS native and GeoDynTools custom algorithms.

The script computes the volume of wastewater generated within each rioleringsgebied (sewerage area) using three primary sources: (1) BAG verblijfsobjecten (residential addresses), applying a configurable 'inw_per_adres' (persons per address) factor and a standard per-capita wastewater generation rate of 12 L/person/hour; (2) VE (verontreinigende emissies, pollution sources) point features, using their 'GRONDSLAG' attribute as a proxy for emission intensity and applying the same 12 L/person/hour rate; and (3) Plancap (planning capacity) polygons, which contribute predefined extra wastewater volumes per time period (2124, 2529, 3039, 4050) in m³/h. It also calculates theoretical POC (punt van ontlasten/point of discharge) volumes from impervious surface area (Gemengd_Aangesloten_ha and Verbeterd_Hemelwater_Aangesloten_ha) using runoff coefficients (0.7 and 0.3). Outputs include: (a) 'DWA_BAG_m3h' — wastewater volume from residential addresses; (b) 'PocBagDrinkwaterVe' — combined POC volume from BAG, drinkwater infrastructure, and VE; (c) 'PlancapPerBem_id' — aggregated extra DWA per rioleringsgebied by planning period; (d) 'Aangesloten_oppervlak_en_poc_eigen_gebied' — impervious area and theoretical POC volume per rioleringsgebied; (e) 'Resultaat_stap2_rioleringsgebieden_met_afvalwateraanbod_uit_eigen_gebied' — final rioleringsgebied layer enriched with all self-sourced wastewater components; and (f) 'BgtIntersectEnOppervlakteAttribuut' — intersected BGT inlooptabel with area and derived ha-based flow components (GEM_ha, HWA_ha, etc.).

The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) features tagged with a user-specified key-value pair (default: 'leisure'='park') within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It downloads OSM data via Overpass API, filters for multipolygon geometries, fixes invalid geometries, clips to the input area, converts multipart geometries to single parts, then filters features whose 'name' field matches case-variant substrings of 'Praca', 'pracinha', 'Largo', or 'Parquinho'. Finally, it refactors attributes into standardized fields including 'nome', 'geometriaAproximada', 'turistica', 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm', and 'nome_osm'. Outputs are two vector layers: one with fixed geometries ('geom') and one filtered and restructured as 'praca_A'.

The script identifies dangles (unconnected line endpoints) in a user-provided vector line layer using the 'Continuous_Network_Analysis:Identify Dangles' algorithm. It then buffers selected project layers (points, lines, and polygons) by 0.000001 decimal degrees, merges the buffered geometries, and performs spatial intersection and non-intersection operations to classify dangles into two outputs: (1) 'DANGLES_Overlapping' — dangles that intersect/overlap with any of the selected layers, and (2) 'DANGLES_Non_Overlap' — dangles that do not intersect/overlap with any selected layer. The output layers preserve original dangle attributes and add a 'layer_overlap' field indicating which overlapping layer contributed to the match.

The script computes and assigns a font size ('tamanho_txt') to river line features based on their length relative to map scale and spatial relationship with a frame polygon. It first adds a unique 'featid' field, merges rivers intersecting the frame using a custom 'mergerivers' algorithm, then calculates label size using ProcessingUtils methods: 'getRiverOutPolyLabelFontSize' for rivers crossing the frame boundary (situacao_em_poligono == 1) and 'getRiverInPolyLabelFontSize' for those fully inside. For 'Carta Ortoimagem' (productParam == 0), minimum size is clamped to 7. Finally, it updates the original drainage layer's 'tamanho_txt' attribute in-place via editing session.

task_name: Extract river headwater points and lines
task_description: The script identifies and extracts river headwaters (springs) from a vector stream network layer using topological dangle detection and length-based filtering. It first dissolves the input line layer, detects dangles (endpoints with degree 1) as candidate headwaters, splits the dissolved network at duplicate vertices (to isolate individual segments), extracts segments intersecting the dangle points, computes segment lengths ($length), filters segments by user-defined length criteria (Minimum Value: ≤ VALUE; Maximum Value: ≥ VALUE; ALL: no filter), removes segments overlapping a buffer around the provided 'River Mouth' point layer (to exclude mouth artifacts), and outputs two results: (1) Headwater_Lines — filtered line segments retaining only a 'Compri' (length) attribute, and (2) Headwater_Points — point features derived from the intersection of original dangles and filtered headwater lines, preserving original layer attributes plus length.

The script validates the geometric and attribute correctness of a user-provided cartographic grid (line layer) and grid numbering points (point layer) against a reference grid generated from a frame polygon and selected map scale. It computes symmetric difference between reference and input grids to identify missing or extraneous grid lines, and performs bidirectional nearest-neighbor joins (within user-defined meter tolerance) between reference and input points to detect missing, incorrectly attributed, or extra grid numbering points. Outputs are two error layers: (1) line features labeled 'erro_grid' representing geometric discrepancies in the grid, and (2) point features labeled 'ponto_faltante', 'ponto_incorreto', or 'ponto_extra' with attributes 'numero' and 'direcao'.

The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) features tagged with 'amenity=police' within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It queries the Overpass API using 'quickosm:buildqueryextent', downloads the response, separates points and multipolygons, clips both to the area of interest, fixes geometries for polygons, buffers clipped polygons by 1e-6 degrees, computes centroids of clipped polygons, extracts points disjoint from the buffered polygons, merges the centroids and disjoint points, calculates an 'osm_id' field prioritizing 'osm_id' over 'osm_way_id', and refactors fields to standardize attribute names ('nome', 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm', 'nome_osm'). The final output is a single vector layer ('Policia_p') containing all extracted police-related point geometries (original points + polygon centroids), with standardized schema and OSM attribution.

The script generates a vector polygon density heatmap by creating a grid (rectangle, diamond, or hexagon) over an input point layer, counting points (optionally weighted by a numeric field) per grid cell, filtering cells by minimum count threshold, and applying a graduated color ramp style based on the count attribute ('NUMPOINTS'). Outputs include a styled vector polygon layer with classified fill colors, optional inversion, outline suppression, and user-configurable grid dimensions, units, color ramp name/mode, and class count.

The script performs spatial joining and aggregation of infrastructure and utility datasets to a drainage basin (bemalingsgebieden) layer. It counts and sums attributes from four input layers: (1) BAG verblijfsobjecten (VBOs) intersecting each basin (count only), (2) VE's (water utility installations) intersecting each basin (count and sum of 'GRONDSLAG'), (3) Drinkwater connections (sum and count of 'zak_result' and 'par_result'), and (4) Plancap polygons (with calculated PC_ID), which are intersected with basins to compute ExAFW values (ExAFW_2124, ExAFW_2529, ExAFW_3039, ExAFW_4050) per basin via area-weighted aggregation after deduplication and ordering by area. Outputs include summary statistics per basin ID (BEM_ID), detection of basins containing multiple plancaps, plancaps overlapping multiple basins, and joined attribute tables for further analysis in the GeoDynGemGWSW workflow.

The script detects pseudo-nodes (line endpoints that are not properly connected to other line vertices) in an input line layer, then determines whether each pseudo-node spatially coincides (topologically connects) with vertices from user-selected vector layers (points, lines, or polygons). It outputs two point layers: (1) 'Pseudo-node Non_Overlap' — pseudo-nodes with no spatial coincidence to any vertex of the selected layers; and (2) 'Pseudo-node Overlapping' — pseudo-nodes that do coincide, enriched with a 'Layer_Name' attribute identifying which source layer contributed the coincident vertex. Vertex extraction is performed per geometry type: points are copied directly; polygon vertices are extracted from outer rings; line vertices are extracted from polylines (including multipart handling). Spatial matching uses QGIS native 'extractbylocation' (predicate=2 → 'contains') and 'intersection' algorithms.

The script performs point sampling on a user-provided vector layer (points) using either random or stratified sampling. For stratified sampling, it classifies the input layer’s numeric field into classes using either quantiles or equal intervals (via a custom QGIS algorithm 'Precision Agriculture:V - Classification'), then performs random selection within each class. The output is a new vector point layer containing the sampled points, with added X and Y coordinate fields.

The script inserts point features representing energy transmission towers along energy transmission lines, clipped to a map frame polygon. It chops the input line layer into segments at regular intervals (scaled by map scale), extracts the start points of each segment, computes rotation angles for symbol orientation, filters out points coincident with line endpoints (boundaries), and populates a target point layer (edicao_simb_torre_energia_p) with those points and attributes (simb_rot, visivel). Finally, it removes any inserted tower points that fall within a user-defined distance (in mm at map scale) from the frame boundary lines.

The script computes a medial axis (skeleton) of an input polygon geometry using a Voronoi-based approach: it generates points along or at vertices of the polygon boundary, constructs Voronoi polygons from those points, converts them to lines, filters line segments lying within the input polygon, dissolves and simplifies the resulting medial axis, optionally applies directional merging to reduce branches, and — if postprocessing is enabled — extracts and extends the longest line segment to intersect with the original polygon boundary. The output is a QgsFeature generator (iterable of QgsFeature objects) representing the final skeleton geometry (or the single longest intersected line after extension and clipping).

The script simplifies a drone flight path defined in a CSV file by reducing the number of waypoints while preserving 3D trajectory fidelity relative to a DEM. It loads CSV points (with longitude, latitude, altitude(m)), samples elevation values from a user-provided DEM raster, reprojects the points to a projected CRS, converts them into a line ordered by 'original_index', simplifies that line using Douglas-Peucker tolerance, extracts vertices of the simplified line, buffers those vertices, joins original reprojected points to the buffers to identify which original points fall within the simplified geometry’s vicinity, and finally filters the input CSV to retain only rows corresponding to those retained indices. Outputs include a simplified CSV file compatible with Litchi, optionally added as a point layer; a trajectory line layer with arrow styling; and original CSV points layer — all configurable via boolean parameters.

task_name: Extract wind turbine locations from OSM
task_description: The script extracts OpenStreetMap (OSM) point features tagged with 'generator:method'='wind_turbine' within a user-defined polygon area of interest. It downloads OSM data via Overpass API, filters for points, clips to the study area, parses the 'height' value from the 'other_tags' field using string operations, and refactors attributes into a standardized output layer with fields: 'nome', 'alturaTorreAer', 'osm_id', 'nome_no_osm', 'geometria_osm', 'nome_osm', and 'alturaTorreAer_osm'. The final output is a vector point layer ('aerogerador_p') containing wind turbine locations and parsed tower height.

The script computes isochrones (travel-time polygons) around candidate retail shops using the ORS Tools plugin, joins census-based demand points (population per LSOA) to those isochrones, aggregates total population demand per shop-time combination (e.g., 'shopID_5' for 5-minute access), and exports a CSV summarizing total demand per shop and travel time threshold. Inputs are local shapefiles: '_demand_points_census.shp' (census LSOA centroids with 'pop2011_al') and 'candidate_shops.shp' (with 'shopID'); output is 'shops_isochrones_demand.csv' containing columns '_shopID', '_AA_MINS', and 'total'.

The script generates spatial tessellations (Thiessen/Voronoi polygons or Delaunay triangulations) from an input point vector layer. For Thiessen/Voronoi methods, it computes the tessellation, derives a convex hull from the input points, and clips the tessellation to that hull. For Delaunay, it performs triangulation and joins attributes from the original points via spatial location. The output is a raster destination layer (though the algorithm logic actually produces vector geometries — indicating a mismatch between parameter type and actual processing, as QgsProcessingParameterRasterDestination is used but all underlying algorithms produce vector layers).

task_name: Prepare building and vegetation height layers
task_description: The script generates two vector layers: (1) a building footprint layer with an added height attribute (ROOF_HEIGHT by default), computed as the median DSM value within each building polygon (optionally adjusted by subtracting DEM to derive above-ground height); and (2) a vegetation layer either rasterized from a canopy DSM (CDSM) — where polygons are created per rounded height class, dissolved by VALUE, and filtered to exclude 0 m — or derived from point data (trunk locations) via buffering using radius/height fields and aspect ratio (0.75 default) to infer missing attributes, then calculating VEG_HEIGHT. Both outputs are vector files (e.g., .shp, .geojson) with user-specified height field names.

The script calculates wastewater discharge prognosis per bemalingsgebied (sewer catchment area) by integrating land use surface runoff characteristics (from BGT inlooptabel), population-based domestic wastewater (from BAG verblijfsobjecten and drinkwater point data), and industrial/commercial wastewater (from VE points). It computes area-based runoff volumes (GEM_ha, VGS_ha, DWA_ha, etc.) using hardening grade and sewer type fractions, then converts to flow rates (m³/h) using standard coefficients (e.g., 0.7 L/s/ha for POC, 12 L/capita/h for DWA). It aggregates direct and overflow (onderbemalingen) contributions across upstream/downstream relationships (NAAR_BEM_ID), sums components (DWA+POC_m3h, DRINKWATER+POC_m3h, VE+POC_m3h), and computes hydraulic metrics: VULTIJD_DWA_MIN_h (minimum filling time) and LEDIGINGSTIJD_h (emptying time) based on BERGING_M3 capacity and total inflow. Outputs include six thematic result layers: POC BAG DRINKWATER, POC BAG DRINKWATER VE, POC_GEM_m3h, POC_VGS_m3h, DWA_BAG_m3/h, and EINDRESULTAAT_HUIDIGE_SITUATIE containing all aggregated flow rates and timing metrics.

The script refactors and standardizes vector geometries (points, lines, or polygons) representing forest implementation areas into a single, validated polygon layer for submission to the Horus monitoring system. It merges input layers, applies topology-aware polygonization (for non-linear inputs) or UTM-zone-specific buffering and reprojection (for linear inputs), dissolves by generated ID, and appends standardized attributes: 'id' (e.g., 'BEL-SP0001-01'), 'culturas' (selected culture list), 'outros' (free-text cultures), 'dt_implant' (implementation date), 'dt_arquivo' (current date), and 'tipo' (fixed value 1 for implemented area). Outputs are reprojected, field-refactored vector features compliant with Horus ingestion requirements.

The script processes spatial layers to delimit sanitation planning subareas by integrating an Area of Interest (AOI) polygon with optional administrative boundaries, existing sanitation system areas, and water availability areas. It performs geometry cleaning (fix geometries, multipart-to-singlepart), union or clipping operations depending on input layer selection, adds standardized attributes (e.g., 'InformalSettlement', 'ExistingSanitation', 'WaterAvailable', 'area_ha', 'uuid'), filters out polygons smaller than a user-defined minimum area (in hectares), and optionally generates a population density grid using either vector or raster population data projected to a target year via exponential growth modeling. Outputs are two vector layers: (1) 'subareas_output_layer' — a cleaned, attributed, and filtered polygon layer representing delimited subareas; and (2) 'population_density_grids' — a gridded vector layer with calculated population density (inhab./ha) for the target year, styled with a predefined QML file.

task_name: Extract forest stand perimeters and associated raster/vector layers
task_description: The script extracts forest stand polygons (TBk_Bestandeskarte), local density vector features, and a 10m canopy height model (VHM) raster clipped to a buffered and dissolved extraction perimeter. It first builds spatial indexes on input vector layers, then extracts TBk_Bestandeskarte features intersecting the user-provided 'Extraction Perimeter', buffers and dissolves those stands twice — once with a user-defined buffer (default 10 m) for raster clipping and once with a tiny buffer (0.0001) for vector containment filtering — then clips the 'vhm_10m' raster using the larger buffered polygon and extracts 'local_densities' features that are fully within the tiny-buffered polygon. Outputs are three geospatial products: a clipped VHM raster ('vhm_10m_extracted'), an extracted TBk stand vector layer ('TBk_Bestandeskarte_extracted'), and an extracted local densities vector layer ('local_densities_extracted').

The script calculates, for each input paddock polygon, the maximum Euclidean distance (in meters) from any point within the paddock to the nearest water point. It does so by: (1) harmonizing CRS between paddock and water point layers (transforming geographic layers to EPSG:9473 if both are geographic, or aligning one to the other’s projected CRS); (2) for each paddock containing ≥1 water point, creating a temporary point layer of intersecting water points; (3) rasterizing those points at user-defined resolution (burn value = 1); (4) computing a GDAL proximity raster (distance in map units); (5) clipping the proximity raster to the paddock geometry; (6) extracting the maximum pixel value (i.e., max distance to water) from the clipped raster; and (7) optionally generating a spreadsheet report listing paddock name, area (ha), water point count, and max distance (km), plus styling and loading proximity rasters with a gradient renderer scaled to the global maximum distance across all paddocks.

task_name: Prepare vector predictors for land cover change modeling
task_description: The script prepares vector datasets for MOLUSCE land cover change modeling by generating a raster aligned to a reference raster’s spatial domain (CRS, extent, rows/columns, pixel alignment). It supports two evidence-based modes: (1) Presence mode — rasterizes vector features (points, lines, polygons), optionally buffered and optionally using a numeric field value or constant 1; (2) Proximity mode — first rasterizes features as binary presence, then computes Euclidean distance to nearest feature, with output units selectable as georeferenced (e.g., meters) or pixels. Output is a single-band raster matching the reference raster’s geometry exactly.

The script buffers input vector features by a user-specified distance, dissolves the resulting polygons, and rasterizes the buffered layer using a specified cell size. Outputs include a vector buffer layer (BUFFER_OUTPUT), a raster layer (OUTPUT) where buffered areas are burned in with value 1 (default behavior of qgis:rasterize), and the count of input features (NUMBEROFFEATURES). All processing is performed locally via QGIS Processing algorithms ('native:buffer' and 'qgis:rasterize'), with no Earth Engine server-side computation — despite the prompt referencing GEE, the script is purely QGIS-based and contains zero ee.* calls or GEE dependencies.

The script creates four standardized polygon vector layers for sanitation planning: Area of Interest (AOI), Administrative Boundaries, Existing Sanitation Area, and Water Availability Area — each with UUID fields, domain-specific attribute fields (e.g., 'SanitationType', 'WaterAvailable', 'AverageWaterConsumption'), default expressions (e.g., 'uuid("Id128")', 'true' for boolean flags), and QGIS .qml style files applied from a project-relative 'Styles/' directory. Optionally, it generates a population density grid by aggregating population data (raster or vector) into user-defined hexagonal/rectangular/diamond grids, projecting to the project CRS, calculating target-year population using exponential growth, and computing population density (persons/km²) as 'popDensity' based on $area.

task_name: Apply direct fuzzifier to indicator raster
task_description: The script applies a linear fuzzy membership transformation to a rasterized indicator layer, using min/max bounds retrieved from the 'Indicators' table in PostGIS. It first constructs a WKT polygon geometry, creates a grid over its extent, joins indicator point values to grid cells via nearest-neighbor, rasterizes the joined grid, applies either direct (min→low, max→high) or inverse (min→high, max→low) linear fuzzification using QGIS's 'fuzzifyrasterlinearmembership', converts the fuzzy raster back to points, appends the indicator_id, and exports the resulting fuzzy points to the 'fuzzy_view' table in PostGIS.

The script identifies flow pathways using a filled DEM and flow accumulation raster via GRASS r.stream.extract, applies a user-defined area threshold (converted from hectares to pixel count), generates flow direction and Strahler order rasters using GRASS r.stream.order, converts the Strahler raster to vector, filters short stream segments (≥3 m), joins Strahler order values to the original stream vector, adds a 'StreamType' field initialized to 5, renames 'cat' → 'Strahler', and removes auxiliary fields ('label', 'stream_typ', 'type_code', 'network'). Outputs include a line vector layer with 'Strahler' and 'StreamType' fields, a streams raster, and a flow direction raster.

The script calculates, for each paddock polygon, the maximum Euclidean distance from any location within that paddock to the nearest water point. It does so by: (1) harmonizing coordinate reference systems between paddock and water point layers; (2) for each paddock, extracting only the water points that intersect it; (3) rasterizing those water points into a binary raster (value 1 at water locations); (4) computing a GDAL proximity raster (distance in map units to nearest pixel with value 1); and (5) clipping the proximity raster to the paddock boundary. The output is a set of clipped proximity rasters — one per paddock containing at least one water point — saved as GeoTIFF files named after the paddock (e.g., 'PaddockA.tif'), where pixel values represent distance in the CRS units (e.g., meters). No aggregation or summary statistics (e.g., max value extraction) is performed beyond raster generation; the rasters themselves are the final outputs.

task_name: Detect forest stand upper layer change
task_description: The script computes two raster outputs: (1) 'change_DG' — a byte raster encoding four states of upper-layer presence/absence change between old and new TBk versions using the formula '(A*10 + B) + 1', where A is old DG (0 or 10) and B is new DG (0 or 1); resulting values are 1 (no upper layer in both), 2 (gain), 11 (loss), 12 (maintain); (2) 'change_DG_hdom' — a byte raster extending change detection to identify cleared areas in stands with hdom_old ≥ thresh_hdom (default 25 m) where hdom reduction exceeds thresh_hdiff (default 7 m), encoded as value 100; all other pixels retain original change_DG codes or are zeroed if hdom_old < threshold. Inputs are vector stand boundaries (with 'hdom' attribute) and co-registered DG rasters for old and new TBk versions.

task_name: Convert raster pixels to point features
task_description: The script converts an input raster layer into vector point features where each pixel becomes a point with its value stored in a 'VALUE' attribute; it then adds an 'indicator_id' field with a user-provided integer value and exports the resulting point layer to a PostGIS table named 'pixels' in the 'integral' database under schema 'public', updating the 'Indicators' table with min/max value statistics and a randomly selected palette code for that indicator_id.

The script computes the USPED (Unit Stream Power-based Erosion Deposition) model output raster, which estimates spatially distributed net erosion/deposition rates. It does so by: (1) computing flow accumulation (using SAGA's top-down MFD algorithm), slope, and aspect from a filled DEM; (2) deriving sflowtopo — a topographic predictor combining flow accumulation and slope with exponentiated sine (rill mode) or linear (sheet mode); (3) multiplying sflowtopo by K-C-R factor rasters (or scalar defaults) and directional cosines/sines of rotated aspect to compute qsx and qsy sediment transport components; (4) computing slope and aspect of qsx and qsy rasters; (5) calculating directional derivatives qsx_dx and qsy_dy using tan(slope) × cos/sin of rotated aspect; and (6) summing the derivatives (with ×10 scaling for sheet erosion mode) to produce the final USPED raster. The Flow Accumulation raster is also output separately.

task_name: Generate stream reach and catchment layers
task_description: The script identifies main stream reaches from an input flow network vector layer using a user-defined numeric field (LimitField) and classification threshold (ClassValue), then rasterizes the selected reaches. It processes D8 flow direction and filled DEM rasters through TauDEM's AreaD8 and StreamNet tools to compute flow accumulation and derive topologically correct stream networks and associated sub-catchments. Outputs are two vector layers: (1) 'Output Stream Reach' — a line layer of stream reaches with original attributes preserved, and (2) 'Output Sub-catchments' — a polygon layer of delineated catchments, dissolved by value, derived from TauDEM's watershed raster output.

task_name: Extract slope and hillshade from DEM
task_description: The script processes a digital elevation model (DEM) raster to generate three derivative rasters: slope in percent, slope in degrees, and hillshade. It uses GDAL's DEMProcessing function with 'slope' and 'hillshade' algorithms, computes edges, and applies specific output file paths. The resulting rasters are loaded into QGIS as layers named 'SLOPE (DEGREE)', 'SLOPE (PERCENT)', and 'HILLSHADE', with the percent-slope layer styled using a predefined QML style. A 10m USGS DEM is optionally loaded if the 1m DEM is not used.

The script samples flood hazard raster layers (e.g., water surface level or inundation depth rasters) against a vector-based exposure inventory (finv) to generate exposure datasets ('expos'). It supports three sampling modes: (1) point-based direct raster value extraction using 'qgis:rastersampling'; (2) polygon/line-based global statistics (e.g., 'Max', 'Mean') via 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' or custom point-along-line + statistics-by-categories workflows; and (3) inundation area/percentage calculation for polygons or lines, requiring a DTM raster and depth threshold — which triggers on-the-fly depth raster generation ('top - bottom'), threshold masking, and zonal pixel counting. Outputs include a vector layer with added raster-derived attribute fields (named after input rasters), optionally saved as CSV, and optional histogram/boxplot visualizations of sampled values.

task_name: Buffer point features for accessibility scoring
task_description: The script performs a single-point buffer workflow to assess accessibility around point features (e.g., facilities or infrastructure) by generating buffered polygons or, for Regional scale, computing percentage overlap between buffers and grid cells (e.g., H3 hexagons) and assigning scores based on configurable thresholds. It supports two scoring modes: binary (presence/absence in buffer → fixed score) and percentage-based (fraction of buffer area intersecting each grid cell → tiered score assignment). Outputs are raster layers aligned to the study area’s bounding box, where pixel values represent assigned scores (e.g., 0–5), intended for integration into multi-criteria spatial assessment frameworks.

The script estimates floodwater depth by subtracting a distance-transformed flood boundary raster (grown from the flood polygon outline) from a clipped DEM, producing a raster where each cell value represents estimated water depth (m) within the inundated area. Key steps include: (1) clipping the input DEM to the flood polygon extent; (2) converting the flood polygon to polyline boundaries; (3) rasterizing those boundaries; (4) extracting DEM elevation values along the rasterized boundary; (5) computing Euclidean distance-to-boundary (i.e., proximity to flood edge) using GRASS r.grow.distance; and (6) calculating depth as max(0, distance-derived surface elevation − clipped DEM), yielding a flood depth raster. A Gaussian-filtered version is also generated but not returned as primary output.

The script identifies potential locations for detainment bunds (DBs), also known as WASCOBs, by processing flow accumulation rasters and stream networks to derive ephemeral/intermittent flow paths within agricultural fields. It generates two outputs: (1) a line vector layer ('PotentialDB') representing candidate DB placements perpendicular to flow direction, filtered by contributing area (2–50 ha), elevation constraints, bank height sufficiency (left/right range > DB height), incision criteria, and exclusion near perennial streams and field boundaries; and (2) a point vector layer ('All DB simulated points') containing all initially spaced candidate points along flow lines, enriched with attributes including contributing area, elevation, azimuth, and DB height — after upstream elevation drop filtering and sorting.

The script performs watershed morphometric analysis by clipping a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to a basin polygon, computing slope statistics, identifying the pour point as the downstream terminus of the highest-order Strahler stream network, calculating basin parameters (e.g., area, perimeter, form factor, relief ratio, hypsometric integral), and generating interpretations for each parameter. Outputs include a vector feature sink containing a table of parameters (name, rounded value, unit, interpretation) anchored at the pour point geometry, plus a hypsometric curve with associated files (e.g., CSV, PNG) saved to a temporary folder.

The script calculates the upslope (contributing) catchment area for each point feature in an input vector layer using a digital elevation model (DEM). It iterates over each point, uses SAGA's 'upslopearea' algorithm to generate a raster catchment mask where cells draining to the point are assigned value 100, then polygonizes that raster and exports only the DN=100 polygons as individual ESRI Shapefiles (one per point) into a user-specified output folder. The workflow relies entirely on local QGIS processing algorithms ('saga:upslopearea' and 'gdal:polygonize') and does not use Earth Engine APIs or remote sensing imagery processing.

task_name: Aggregate GeoE3 scores by subnational boundaries
task_description: The script calculates majority-class GeoE3 Score (5 classes: 0–5) and GeoE3 × Population Score (15 classes) for each subnational administrative polygon using zonal statistics (majority mode) on precomputed VRT rasters. It processes up to four raster inputs — 'GeoE3_Score_combined.vrt', 'geoe3_by_population_score.vrt', 'geoe3_score_ghsl_masked.vrt', and 'geoe3_score_by_population_ghsl_masked.vrt' — against a user-provided aggregation vector layer (e.g., provinces or districts). Outputs are GeoPackage layers with columns 'fid', 'name', 'geoe3_score', and 'geoe3_pop_score', styled with QML files ('geoe3_score_vector.qml' and 'geoe3_by_population_vector_score.qml'). Geometry is pre-processed via 'native:fixgeometries' and field-retention to preserve 'fid'.

The script computes the difference raster 'diff_hdom_vhm' by subtracting a rasterized stand-level hdom (height dominant) attribute — derived from the vector layer 'tbk_bestandesgrenzen' (forest stand boundaries) — from the input VHM_10m (vegetation height model at 10 m resolution). It also generates a point layer 'vhm_10m_points' by converting each pixel of the VHM_10m raster to a point with its value. The workflow uses GDAL rasterize (with hdom field, 10 m resolution, Float32), GDAL raster calculator (B − A, where B is VHM_10m and A is rasterized hdom), and QGIS native pixel-to-points conversion.

The script delineates nested hydrologic subregions (subbasins) from a digital elevation model (DEM), iteratively tuning the flow accumulation threshold to achieve a target number of subbasins (9–13), then integrates lake features into the watershed network, computes bankfull channel geometry parameters (k and c), generates outlet/inlet point vectors and catchment polygon masks per subregion, and finally merges subregion results into a unified, topologically consistent watershed hierarchy with updated drainage area, Strahler order, and routing attributes. Key outputs include packed GRASS rasters (FDR, ACC, STR_R, STR_V, DEM), shapefiles for subregion masks (HyMask_region_*.shp), outlet/inlet points (Sub_Reg_Outlet_v.shp, sub_reg_inlet.shp), subregion metadata (Sub_reg_info.csv), and combined final catchments (finalcat_info.shp) and rivers (finalcat_info_riv.shp).

task_name: Compute zonal statistics for environmental variables
task_description: The script computes zonal statistics (mean, min, max, std, etc.) of a continuous environmental raster variable within buffered zones (circular buffers) around species occurrence points. It first creates buffers around input point features using a user-defined radius, then calculates 12 statistical metrics (including mean, median, std dev, min, max, range, sum, count, variance, minority, majority, and variety) over each buffer using the 'native:zonalstatisticsfb' algorithm, and finally derives centroids of the buffered polygons to retain point geometry with attached statistics. The output is a point vector layer ('EstadisticasDeCitas') where each original occurrence point is replaced by its buffer centroid and enriched with raster-derived statistics prefixed by 'Sta_'.

The script rasterizes a categorical environmental vector layer (e.g., land cover, soil type, or administrative zoning) into a standardized-resolution raster aligned to territorial influence boundaries for Maxent modeling. It first extracts the input vector layer by location using a hardcoded polygon layer ('Limite_Demarcacion_Ebro_c837559a_0494_4177_882f_71dd55fdeb90'), then rasterizes the clipped vector using a numeric field containing categorical values, and finally clips the resulting raster to the provided territorial boundary layer with user-specified pixel resolution. The output is a single-band categorical raster in GeoTIFF format, ready for Maxent species distribution modeling.

The script calculates a masked GeoE3 Score raster by multiplying a per-study-area job opportunities mask raster (values 0 or 1) with the corresponding GeoE3 Score raster (range 0–5, five enablement classes). It processes each study area iteratively using QgsRasterLayer inputs, validates alignment (extent and dimensions), applies raster algebra via GDAL's raster calculator ('A * B'), saves individual masked rasters (e.g., 'geoe3_score_ghsl_masked_0.tif'), then combines them into a single VRT file ('geoe3_score_ghsl_masked.vrt'). A QML style file ('analysis.qml') is copied to the output directory to render the five-class color legend (#FF0000, #FFA500, #FFFF00, #90EE90, #0000FF). Inputs are sourced from pre-existing folders: 'opportunity_masks' (binary masks) and 'geoe3_score' (GeoE3 Score rasters), both indexed by study area index.

The script reclassifies an input environmental hazards raster (e.g., fire, flood, landslide, cyclone, or drought) into a standardized 0–5 severity scale using layer-specific threshold rules. It loads the raster via QgsRasterLayer, applies QGIS native 'reclassifybytable' with predefined min/max/value triplets per hazard type, clips the result to the study area’s mask layer, and saves the output as a GeoTIFF (e.g., 'fire_reclassified_0.tif') in the workflow directory. The reclassification logic is hardcoded per layer_id and uses range boundaries (e.g., 2 for landslide, 0 otherwise), and logging confirms rule application and file output.

task_name: Convert raster pixels to point features
task_description: The script converts a raster input layer into point vector features, reprojects it to EPSG:3857, clips it to a user-provided polygon study area, adds a static integer field 'project_indicator_id' (supplied as a parameter) to each point, and exports the resulting point layer to a PostGIS table named 'pixels' in the 'public' schema of the 'integral' database. The output is not a new raster or statistical summary but a persisted spatial table of pixel centroids with indicator metadata.

task_name: Compute LS factor for erosion modeling
task_description: The script computes the LS factor (topographic factor in RUSLE/USPED erosion models) from a filled DEM raster. It first calculates slope (in degrees) using the native QGIS slope algorithm, then computes flow accumulation using SAGA's 'Flow Accumulation (Top-Down)' with Multiple Flow Direction method (METHOD=4), and finally applies a raster calculator expression: (m * (flow_accumulation / 22.1)^m * (sin(slope_radians / 0.09))^n), where m is the sheet erosion factor (0.4–0.6) and n is the rill erosion factor (1.0–1.3). Outputs are three rasters: LS factor map, slope map, and flow accumulation map.

The script estimates floodwater depth from a flood extent polygon and a digital elevation model (DEM) using a multi-step geoprocessing workflow: (1) it fixes geometries of the input inundation polygon; (2) converts the polygon to polylines; (3) clips the DEM to the inundation polygon; (4) rasterizes the flood boundary polyline at the DEM’s native resolution; (5) extracts underlying DEM elevations along the boundary using raster multiplication and division; (6) applies GRASS7's r.grow.distance to compute Euclidean distance-based elevation interpolation (nearest boundary elevation assigned to interior cells); (7) computes preliminary water depth as the difference between interpolated flood level and clipped DEM, zeroing negative values; and (8) applies SAGA's Gaussian low-pass filter for smoothing. Outputs include a raw water depth raster ('waterDepth.tif') and a smoothed version ('*_low_pass.tif'), optionally saved to user-specified paths.

The script identifies candidate road alignment points based on slope values (in degrees) extracted from a precomputed slope raster (1820_SLOPE(DEGREE).tif), filters them into five slope ranges (0–24°, 24–32°, 32–40°, 40–45°, and 0–45°), writes each as point shapefiles, then excludes points within a 10-meter buffer of existing streams (1820_Streams-2225.shp) to generate a final 'GENERATED ROAD POINTS.shp' layer containing only slope-appropriate, stream-distant candidate road points.

The script converts vector polygon layers representing species range distributions into individual species-specific raster maps. It first adds a presence field (named 'presence' by default, populated with value 1) to the input polygon layer using QGIS field calculator; then iterates over unique values in the user-specified attribute field (e.g., species name), selects features per species, saves each as a separate shapefile, and rasterizes each into a GeoTIFF with fixed dimensions (2000×1000 pixels), using the presence field for pixel values. Outputs are one GeoTIFF per species, named after the species value (with spaces replaced by underscores), saved to the specified output directory.

The script computes the number of distinct languages (from the 'wlds_cleaned.shp' dataset) intersecting each country polygon (from 'ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp'), producing a CSV file ('nlangs_country.csv') with one row per country (ADMIN field) and a count of associated language features (GID). It uses QGIS Processing algorithms: geometry fixing on both inputs, intersection between language polygons and country boundaries, then categorical statistics (count) grouped by country name (ADMIN). No classification, modeling, or temporal analysis is performed — only spatial aggregation and counting.

task_name: Extract forest stand data by perimeter
task_description: The script extracts forest stand vector and raster datasets from the TBk (Bestandeskarte) inventory dataset using a user-defined extraction perimeter (a GeoPackage polygon layer). It first filters the main stand layer (TBk_Bestandeskarte.shp) by spatial intersection with the perimeter, then creates two buffered/dissolved versions of the extracted stands: a tightly buffered (0.0001°) version for vector-layer clipping (using 'are within' predicate), and a coarsely buffered (10 m) version for raster clipping (using GDAL's cliprasterbymasklayer). All listed vector datasets (e.g., TBk_local_densities.gpkg, stands_simplified.shp) and raster datasets (e.g., dg_layer.tif, VHM_10m.tif, classified_smooth_2.tif) are clipped to their respective buffered perimeters. Outputs include the filtered stand layer and all clipped vector/raster layers written to the specified output directory.

task_name: Extract NDVI vegetation statistics for plot
task_description: The script processes a list of JSON configuration objects to extract NDVI-based vegetation statistics (count, mean, standard deviation) for a user-specified plot ID within an input vector layer (plots). It first selects the target plot by attribute value, buffers it inward by 10 units (negative buffer), calculates a masked NDVI raster where only pixels with band A@3 values equal to 4 or 5 are retained (else NoData), and then computes zonal statistics of that NDVI raster over the buffered plot geometry. The final output is a shapefile containing the original plot geometry augmented with NDVI statistics fields (e.g., 'mean', 'std'), written to the path specified in the JSON's OUTPUTS section.

task_name: Calculate Curve Number from land cover and soil data
task_description: The script calculates the Soil Conservation Service (SCS) Curve Number (CN) raster for a user-defined polygon study area using two global datasets: ESA WorldCover 2021 (land cover classification) and ORNL HYSOG (hydrologic soil groups). It processes these rasters by clipping to the study area extent, aligning their spatial resolution and extent, performing a pixel-wise lookup using a CSV-based CN table indexed by land cover code and soil group (A/B/C/D → 1/2/3/4), and applying hydrologic condition (Poor/Fair/Good) and antecedent runoff condition (I/II/III) parameters. Outputs include an optional ESA land cover raster, an optional soil group raster, and a mandatory final CN raster clipped to the input polygon. The script also computes and reports mean CN, potential retention (S), and direct runoff (Q) statistics.

The script generates a Curve Number (CN) raster layer for a user-defined Area of Interest (AOI) by combining ESA WorldCover 2021 land cover data and ORNL Hydrologic Soil Groups (HYSOGs250m) soil data. It optionally outputs aligned rasters (ESA Land Cover, HSG), the final CN raster, and a vectorized CN layer via polygonization. When no custom lookup table is provided, it selects a precomputed CSV lookup (e.g., 'default_lookup_f_ii.csv') based on user-selected Hydrologic Condition (HC) and Antecedent Runoff Condition (ARC). The CN computation uses raster algebra ('perform_raster_math') mapping ESA LC codes + HSG values to CN values via a grid_code → cn mapping. Areas with missing ORNL soil data (e.g., permanent water) default to HSG D. All processing uses GDAL-based clipping, warping, translation, and polygonization within QGIS Processing Framework.

The script computes Land Surface Temperature (LST) and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from Landsat 7 bands: B3 (red), B4 (NIR), and B6 (thermal infrared). It first converts B6 digital numbers to at-sensor radiance using the gain/offset parameters (gain = (12.650 − 3.200)/(255 − 1), offset = 3.200), then applies a single-channel LST inversion: LST = (1282.71 / ln(666.09 / L) + 1) − 273.15 (Kelvin to Celsius), where L is the radiance. NDVI is calculated as (B4 − B3) / (B4 + B3). Both outputs are clipped to a user-provided ROI polygon and styled with QGIS layer styles (NDVI_style_new.qml, LST_style_new.qml).

The script performs hydrological conditioning of a digital elevation model (DEM) by optionally resampling it, carving stream networks using blue-line vector data (with user-defined depth), and inserting artificial walls (barriers) using wall vector data. It then computes flow accumulation and extracts stream networks based on a user-specified threshold in km², converted to cell count using the DEM's ground resolution. Outputs include: (1) raw DEM (_DEMraw.tif), (2) conditioned DEM (_DEMconditioned.tif), and (3) extracted stream raster (_streams.tif). All operations use GRASS GIS and GDAL algorithms within QGIS Processing Framework.

task_name: Clip raster and compute zonal histogram
task_description: The script clips a raster layer using a polygon vector mask and then computes a zonal histogram for the clipped raster within each polygon feature. The output is a vector layer (polygon) with added histogram band count columns prefixed 'HISTO_' (e.g., HISTO_1, HISTO_2), derived from the first band of the clipped raster. No classification, thresholding, or temporal aggregation occurs; it is strictly a spatial clipping + per-polygon histogram tabulation workflow.

task_name: Split RGB bands from input image
task_description: The script splits an input raster image into its Red, Green, and Blue spectral bands using SAGA's 'splitrgbbands' algorithm, then converts each extracted band (R, G, B) to a standardized format via GDAL Translate—preserving CRS and data type—producing six outputs: three raw band rasters (BLUE, GREEN, RED) and three converted rasters (R_conv, G_conv, B_conv). The workflow is strictly band decomposition and format conversion; no spectral index calculation, classification, or temporal/spatial filtering is performed.

The script computes impeded flow depth by subtracting an unfilled (hydroconditioned) DEM from a filled DEM, then filters the difference raster to retain only positive values (i.e., locations where filling raised the surface — indicating depressions that impede flow). The output is a raster named 'Impeded flow' (DepthGrid), where cell values represent the depth of impeded flow (in elevation units matching the input DEMs); all non-positive differences are set to zero.

task_name: Reproject and clip raster to mask extent
task_description: The script reprojects a source raster to match the coordinate reference system and spatial properties (cell size, CRS) of a mask raster, then clips the reprojected raster using a vector mask layer (shapefile). Outputs are two GeoTIFF files: one reprojected ('_proj.tif') and one clipped to the mask geometry ('.tif'), both stored in the GRASS database directory. The workflow uses QGIS Processing algorithms 'gdal:warpreproject' and 'gdal:cliprasterbymasklayer', with no resampling or nodata handling specified, and exits QGIS cleanly after execution.

The script computes a composite environmental suitability index (1–4) for educational infrastructure siting by integrating three reprojected, classified raster inputs: Multi-Hazard Risk (1–4, inverted weight), slope-derived elevation suitability (1–4 via slope thresholds: <1°=1, 1–10°=2, 10–20°=3, ≥20°=4), and forest/vegetation suitability (binary input inverted to 1 if not dense forest, else 4). It applies user-defined weights (summing to 1.0), merges weighted layers via linear combination, and optionally clips the result to a user-provided polygon study area. The output is a single-band raster where value 1 = *More suitable* and 4 = *Less suitable*, explicitly contradicting typical hazard indexing conventions per the help string.

The script downloads a selected Copernicus Global Land product (e.g., 'CGLS_LAI300', 'CGLS_FAPAR1K') by dynamically scraping the VITO land.copernicus.vgt.vito.be/manifest/ directory to list available collections, then retrieves the manifest for the selected collection, parses it to find the NetCDF file with the date closest to the user-specified day, downloads that NetCDF file, identifies its first subdataset using GDAL, opens it as a QgsRasterLayer, and converts it to a compressed GeoTIFF (DEFLATE, PREDICTOR=2, ZLEVEL=9) using GDAL Translate. Outputs include the final GeoTIFF file and the original downloaded NetCDF URL.

The script combines multiple input raster layers using user-defined weights, optionally normalizes them, reprojects them to a common projected CRS, merges them into a single weighted sum raster, clips the result to a study area polygon if provided, and samples the resulting hazard index raster at school point locations. Outputs include the final combined raster and a vector layer of schools with sampled hazard index values.

The script computes zonal statistics (mean values) for raster datasets—land quality, and population density for years 1500 AD, 1990 AD, and 2000 AD—using country boundaries (ne_10m_admin_0_countries.shp) as zones. It fixes geometries, drops all attribute fields except 'ADMIN' and 'ISO_A3', appends zonal statistics prefixed by 'lqua_', 'pd15_', 'pd19_', and 'pd20_' to the vector layer, then exports the resulting attribute table—including original country fields plus computed statistics—to a CSV file at 'C:/Users/se.4537/Dropbox/PoliteconGIS/LBS_2020/PhD/lecture_3/gis_data/_output/country_level_zs.csv'.

The script downloads 84 individual orthophoto ZIP files from the official Vienna city portal (ma41), unzips them, reprojects each TIFF from EPSG:31256 (MGI / Austria Lambert) to EPSG:4326 (WGS84), merges all reprojected TIFFs into a single ortho.jpg raster, and updates the QGIS project with this merged orthophoto layer. All operations are hardcoded for Vienna's administrative grid tiles (e.g., '22_4', '32_2'), and file paths are fixed to local macOS user directory '/Users/arthurrufhosangdacosta/qgis_data/temp/ortho/'. The final output is a georeferenced, globally aligned orthophoto mosaic of Vienna.

The script generates a Curve Number (CN) raster layer for a user-defined Area of Interest (AOI) within the contiguous United States (CONUS) by combining NLCD 2021 Land Cover and SSURGO soil data. It first reprojects the AOI to EPSG:5070, computes bounding box with buffer, downloads NLCD 2021 Land Cover and Impervious Surface rasters via WMS/WCS from mrlc.gov, and retrieves SSURGO soil polygons via POST or WFS requests (with XY swap correction and geometry fixing). It then polygonizes NLCD land cover, simplifies soil hydrologic groups (optionally removing '/D' suffix for drained soils), joins land cover codes with soil hydrologic soil group (HSG) codes using a lookup table (default or custom CSV), and computes CN values based on the concatenated 'land_cover_HSG' key. Optional outputs include NLCD Land Cover raster, NLCD Impervious Surface raster, and SSURGO soil vector layer — all reprojected to the AOI's original CRS.

The script adds a new text field 'description' to an input vector layer by executing a user-defined Python function that maps feature attributes (via a dictionary of field names and values) to a descriptive string; it also adds a second text field 'metadata' containing a JSON-serialized dictionary built from user-provided key-value pairs in a matrix parameter. The output is a new vector layer with these two additional fields.

The script cleans and standardizes a vector layer of language boundaries (langa.shp) by fixing invalid geometries, adding a unique autoincremental GID field, copying the 'NAME_PROP' attribute into a shorter 'lnm' field, and dropping all other attributes except 'GID', 'ID', and 'lnm'. The final output is a simplified shapefile 'wlds_cleaned.shp' containing only those three fields and topologically valid geometries.

The script interpolates elevation values from a digital elevation model (DEM) raster layer onto a pixel-center-aligned vector grid, then reprojects the grid and generates a new raster using TIN interpolation with linear method. The output is a resampled elevation raster at a specified pixel size, aligned to the input extent and CRS.

The script performs topological connectivity analysis on a line vector layer (e.g., river or stream network) relative to an initial input layer and a 'River Mouth' point/geometry layer. It iteratively selects connected features by spatial adjacency (using 'intersects' predicate), starting from features intersecting the River Mouth, then expanding selection to all lines sharing vertices (via vertex extraction, dissolve by ID, and repeated select-by-location). The workflow outputs two vector layers: (1) 'Excerpt Disconnected' — line segments *not* topologically connected to the River Mouth via the network; and (2) 'Connected section' — line segments that *are* topologically connected. The algorithm relies entirely on vector geometry operations (vertex extraction, dissolve, select-by-location, extract-by-location) and does not use raster or time-series data.

The script configures the 'sobreposto' (overlaid) and 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' (show approximate label) attributes of the legal boundary line layer ('llp_limite_legal_l') based on spatial relationships with filtered infrastructure and drainage layers. It first filters drenagem, via_deslocamento, and ferrovia layers by 'visivel' = 1 (and 'situacao_em_poligono' = 1 for drenagem), merges them, computes their intersection and difference with the legal boundary layer after subtracting the moldura (frame) polygon boundary (converted to lines), then replaces all features in the input legal boundary layer: intersecting features are assigned 'sobreposto' = 1 and 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' = 1; non-intersecting (difference) features are assigned 'sobreposto' = 2 and 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' = 1. The operation is performed in-place via editing session on the input vector layer.

The script performs vector geometry cleaning on an input vector layer by sequentially applying geometry repair, polygon dissolution, multipart-to-singlepart conversion, hole removal (for holes < 20 m²), topology-preserving simplification (with user-defined tolerance in meters), and iterative smoothing (with user-defined iterations and offset). The output is a cleaned, simplified, and smoothed single-part polygon vector layer with topological integrity preserved and small artifacts removed.

The script computes the largest empty circle (LEC) for a given point layer: it identifies the center point farthest from any input point (i.e., the Voronoi vertex with maximum minimum distance to sites), then generates a circular buffer of radius equal to that maximum distance.
