The workflow uses QGIS native processing algorithms — first computing the LEC center via an external `lec()` function (imported from `becagislibrary.voronoi`), then applying `qgis:deleteduplicategeometries` to clean the center geometry, and finally `native:buffer` to create the circular polygon output. Outputs are two vector layers: (1) a point layer representing the center of the LEC, and (2) a single dissolved polygon layer representing the largest empty circle itself. Radius handling includes optional geographic CRS correction using Gaussian mean Earth radius derived from WGS84 ellipsoid parameters.

task_name: Optimize spatial join for forest stand mapping
task_description: The script performs an optimized spatial join between two vector layers: a primary 'layer to join attribute on' and a secondary 'attribute layer' (expected to be polygonal, e.g., vegetation zones). It ensures performance by first checking and creating a spatial index on the primary layer if missing; converting the secondary layer to singlepart geometries; fixing geometries using the 'Structure' method; indexing the resulting singlepart layer; and finally executing a one-to-one spatial join ('largest overlap only') with intersection predicate. Outputs a vector layer identical in geometry to the primary layer but enriched with selected attributes from the secondary layer, prefixed as specified (e.g., 'VegZone_'). The workflow is explicitly designed for the TBk (Toolkit Bestandeskarte) QGIS plugin used in forest stand map generation.

The script connects to a SQLite-based Talsim hydrological simulation database, loads scenario-specific SystemElement data (points), SubBasin (polygons), and TransportReach (lines) layers into QGIS as memory layers with symbology, enables interactive editing of geometries and attributes, and synchronizes changes back to the database. It supports inserting new elements, updating existing geometries/attributes, updating coordinates from geometry centroids, and loading external polygon/line layers to update or insert sub-basins and transport reaches. Outputs include QGIS vector layers (SystemElements, Outflows, Sub-basins, TransportReach, Updated Elements) grouped under a scenario-named layer group, with real-time bidirectional sync between QGIS edits and the SQLite DB.

The script generates an oriented vector grid aligned with the dominant direction of points in an input point layer, where point order reflects data acquisition sequence (e.g., along crop rows or machine pass). It computes the median heading angle from consecutive point pairs, rotates a buffered extent-based grid around the centroid by the negative of that angle, and outputs the rotated grid as a vector layer. The grid cell size is user-defined in meters, and manual rotation override is supported.

The script configures topological overlap status for a line layer ('edicao_limite_especial_l') by intersecting and differencing it against filtered and merged infrastructure layers (drenagem, via deslocamento, ferrovia) clipped to a dissolved moldura polygon boundary. It updates the input line layer in-place: features intersecting the merged infrastructure are assigned 'sobreposto' = 1; non-intersecting portions are assigned 'sobreposto' = 2; both receive 'exibir_rotulo_aproximado' = 1. The workflow includes visibility/situation filtering, dissolve, clip, polygon-to-line conversion, intersection, and difference operations using QGIS native algorithms.

The script converts a QGIS vector layer representing field boundaries and weed patches into an AGOpenGPS-compatible Sections.txt file. It constructs a hierarchical grid (small and large quadrats), computes the applied area as the field boundary minus weed polygons, extracts grid cells fully inside the non-weed area, performs geometric difference between small and large grids to avoid overlap, merges resulting polygons (large-grid sections, small-grid-only sections, and boundary-aligned small-grid sections), and exports each polygon as a 5-line entry in the Sections.txt format: first line '5' (vertex count), second line RGB color, followed by four WGS84 vertices converted to local easting/northing relative to a StartFix coordinate read from the AOG Fields.txt file. The output includes both a QGIS vector layer ('Sections Layer') and the ASCII Sections.txt file.

The script processes municipal sewer network data to derive asset-level characteristics for drainage areas and outflow points. It starts by spatially joining sewer network elements (knooppunten/points, kunstwerken/structures, verbindingen/lines) with rioleringsgebieden (sewer catchment polygons), then creates Stelsel_ID identifiers by buffering sewer lines and intersecting with catchments. Key outputs include: (1) Rioolgemalen (pumping stations) with attributes like Afvoercapaciteit_m3h, Inslagpeil_mNAP, Uitslagpeil_mNAP; (2) Stelsel_ID_kenmerken_kunstwerken containing counts and minima of doorlaatniveau/drempelniveau per Stelsel_ID; (3) Leidingberging_m3 and Knooppuntberging_m3 calculated using geometry (VormLeiding, BreedteLeiding, HoogteLeiding, LengteLeiding, VormPut, BreedtePut, Lengteput) and elevation logic (BobBeginpuntLeiding, BobEindpuntLeiding, Maaiveldhoogte_Q1_mNAP, Laagste_Drempelniveau_mNAP); (4) Resultaat_stap1_afvoerrelatie (outflow relationships between pumping stations and discharge points); (5) Resultaat_stap1_rioolstelsels (aggregated system-level storage volumes); (6) Resultaat_stap1_afvoerpunten (outflow points with system attributes); (7) Lozingspunten_rioolgemalen (discharge points); (8) Resultaat_stap1_afvoerboom (catchment-to-catchment flow tree). All calculations are based on local Dutch sewer asset conventions (e.g., mNAP vertical datum, specific formulas for egg-shaped vs rectangular pipe volume, 0.6 m freeboard below maaiveld).

The script filters and relocates point structures (e.g., bridges, culverts) from MTMD and road–river intersections to produce a cleaned point layer of infrastructure features within 100 m of the hydrographic network. It does so by: (1) computing line intersections between river and road networks; (2) merging those intersections with MTMD point structures; (3) buffering merged points by 2 m; (4) dissolving overlapping buffers; (5) computing centroids of dissolved buffers to aggregate nearby features; (6) extracting only those centroids within 100 m of the river network; and (7) assigning a unique integer ID ('fid') to each resulting point. The output is a vector point layer named 'New_structure' containing filtered, aggregated, and uniquely identified infrastructure points proximal to rivers.

The script identifies the most isolated point in an input point layer by computing pairwise distances and selecting the point with the maximum minimum distance to any other point. It outputs (1) a single-point vector layer containing that isolated point, and (2) a circular buffer around it with radius equal to that maximum minimum distance — converted from meters to degrees if the input CRS is geographic. The isolation computation is performed by the external `isolation()` function (imported from `becagis.becagislibrary.voronoi`), which returns the unique field value identifying the isolated point and the corresponding distance value.

The script extracts and exports Portuguese administrative units (freguesia, concelho, distrito) from the CAOP vector dataset, clipped to a user-defined Area de Trabalho. It performs spatial filtering (extract by location), identifies unique concelhos and distritos, refactors attribute fields (e.g., adding 'inicio_objeto' with current timestamp and 'data_publicacao' from parameter), dissolves geometries by administrative codes (dicofre for freguesia, left(Dicofre,2) for distrito, left(Dicofre,4) for concelho), and imports the resulting layers into PostgreSQL tables ('freguesia', 'distrito', 'concelho') under schema 'public' using GDAL's PostGIS import tool. All outputs are vector polygon layers with standardized field schemas and geometry columns named 'geometria'.

The script extracts the edges of input polygon geometries by buffering the polygon boundaries inward and outward by half the specified width (in tenths of millimeter), then computing the difference between the external and internal buffers to produce a new polygon layer representing the edge strip. The output is a vector layer with an added 'h' attribute set to braille.DIM['f'], and all intermediate geometries are processed through multipart-to-singlepart conversion, geometry fixing, and simplification at 0.0001 m tolerance.

task_name: Smooth Voronoi polygons by jittering vertices
task_description: The script generates smoothed Voronoi tessellations from input point features, constrained to a base polygon layer (e.g., country or administrative boundary). It first computes standard Voronoi polygons, clips them to the base map, densifies polygon boundaries with additional vertices, randomly perturbs each vertex within a user-defined tolerance, reconstructs closed polygon paths from the jittered vertices, buffers the resulting lines to fill gaps, clips again to the base map, and finally joins original point attributes back to the smoothed polygons. The output is a vector layer of smoothed, topologically valid Voronoi-derived polygons retaining original point identifiers and attributes.

The script performs a light geometric cleanup on an input vector layer by (1) removing features with null or empty geometries directly from the original layer and logging their IDs and attributes to a no-geometry output table, and (2) removing duplicate vertices from line and polygon features using QGIS's native:removeduplicatevertices algorithm. It does not fix or delete invalid geometries. The output includes the modified input layer (in-place edits) and a separate attribute-only table containing the deleted features' original attributes plus auxiliary fields 'lf_orig_id' and 'lf_reason'.

The script generates a UTM-based cartographic grid vector layer clipped to a user-provided frame polygon, with optional latitude/longitude tick marks (crosses at minute intervals) and grid numbering points (E/N direction labels with two-digit numbers derived from UTM coordinates modulo 100). The grid spacing is scale-dependent (e.g., 4×5000/100 = 200 m for 1:5,000), master lines occur every 10th interval, and output layers are reprojected to the appropriate SIRGAS 2000 UTM zone determined by the frame centroid. Outputs include a line layer (grid + ticks) and an optional point layer (grid numbers).

The script computes the areal average precipitation over a catchment by spatially intersecting a gridded precipitation dataset with the catchment boundary, calculating cell areas, assigning weights as the ratio of each cell's area to the total catchment area, and then computing weighted precipitation values (e.g., DATA_20200101_pesata) for each precipitation time step field. Outputs include: (1) clipped grid intersecting the catchment, (2) reprojected precipitation grid (EPSG:32632), (3) clipped grid with added fields 'area_cella', 'area_bacino_const', and 'peso', and (4) final vector layer with weighted precipitation fields appended.

The script places master contour line labels for Brazilian topographic mapping by identifying contour lines whose elevation values are multiples of a scale-dependent index (e.g., 50 m at 1:25,000), extracting QGIS-rendered label bounding polygons from map layers within geographic boundaries, clipping master contours against those label polygons, splitting and buffering interpolated midpoints to isolate candidate label placement segments, and populating a dedicated symbol layer (edicao_simb_cota_mestra_l) with geometry and elevation values while clearing the 'texto_edicao' attribute on original contour lines. Outputs include updated contour layer attributes and new features in the contour symbol layer.

The script divides input polygon parcels into smaller lots of a specified width (LOT_WIDTH) using geometric division lines derived from shortest polygon sides and oriented minimum bounding boxes for irregular polygons. It identifies regular (rectangular, 5-vertex) polygons directly and computes oriented minimum bounding boxes for irregular ones; then constructs horizontal division lines between midpoints of the two shortest sides, generates perpendicular lot-divider lines spaced at the desired lot width (with optional uniform corner distribution), extends all lines by 5 cm, clips them to the original parcel boundaries, splits the input parcels along those lines, and performs two iterative passes of merging small resulting polygons (below MERGE_THRESHOLD % of average area) based on shared boundary length. The output is a new vector layer of divided parcels with merged small lots.

The script merges line features representing river segments (from a drainage layer) that share the same 'nome' (name) attribute and are topologically connected (intersecting geometries). It first adds an auto-increment field, creates a spatial index, dissolves the frame polygon layer, clips the drainage layer to the dissolved frame, merges lines by name using geometric combination and mergeLines(), converts the frame polygon to lines, splits the merged lines at frame boundaries, and outputs a new MultiLineString layer with merged river segments preserving original attributes. The merging logic prioritizes longer segments per name group and iteratively combines intersecting features with identical names.

The script processes a vector layer representing a sewer network (e.g., drainage basins or pumping stations) to compute upstream accumulation of wastewater flows and undercapacity metrics. It constructs a directed graph from network topology fields (e.g., 'Bemalingsgebied_ID' → 'Bemalingsgebied_ID_Lozingspunt'), identifies upstream nodes using Dijkstra’s algorithm, aggregates flow-related fields (e.g., 'DWA_BAG_m3h', 'Drinkwater_Totaal_m3h') from upstream contributors, and computes derived undercapacity fields including 'POC_Praktijk_Onderbem_DWA_obv_BAG_m3h', 'Afvalwateraanbod_obv_BAG_En_POC_Praktijk_m3h', and 'Sommatie_POC_Praktijk_DWA_obv_BAG_m3h_obv_afvoercap'. Outputs include updated vector layers with new attribute fields, grouped into 'hoofdresultaten' (main results) and 'tussenresultaten' (intermediate results), optionally saved as GeoPackage files and styled with QML files.

The script merges two polygon vector layers representing agricultural zonings (e.g., management zones, soil zones, or yield zones) using geometric union and topology cleanup. It first repairs geometries of both input layers, performs a vector union operation to compute their spatial intersection and overlay, converts multipart features to singleparts, adds geometry attributes (area, perimeter), and appends a unique auto-incremented ZONE_ID field. The output is a single vector layer where each polygon represents a non-overlapping atomic zone resulting from the logical combination of the two input zonings.

The script computes the density of overlapping polygons by performing a vector union operation on an input polygon layer, then aggregating count statistics (and optionally concatenating unique IDs) per resulting geometry fragment. It optionally filters output polygons to retain only those with overlap counts greater than or equal to a user-specified threshold. The output is a polygon feature class where each feature represents a non-overlapping geometric fragment and carries an attribute 'NUMPOINTS' indicating how many original input polygons overlapped that fragment, plus optionally an 'ID_LIST' field listing the unique IDs of contributing polygons.

The script splits a vector layer of labeled samples into two disjoint subsets: a training subset (containing a user-specified percentage, default 70%, of randomly selected features) and a test subset (containing the remaining features), using QGIS native algorithms 'randomextract' and 'difference'. The outputs are two vector feature sinks—'TrainSubset' and 'TestSubset'—each preserving the original geometry and attributes of the input 'Samples' layer.

task_name: Calculate scenario-based land area by administrative unit
task_description: The script processes multiple input vector layers (e.g., land use or hazard scenario maps), clips each to a mask layer, intersects with functional administrative units (e.g., municipalities), computes area in km² per intersected polygon, aggregates total area per unit (grouped by ISTAT code), and joins results back to the administrative layer — producing a single output vector layer where each administrative unit carries summed area values for each input scenario (e.g., 'alta', 'media', 'bassa' derived from the 'per' field), alongside attributes like ISTAT, Comune, and Provincia.

The script computes the convex hull polygon enclosing all input point features. It first dissolves the input point layer (though dissolution has no effect on points without grouping fields), then applies QGIS's native convex hull algorithm to generate a single polygon output representing the minimal convex envelope around the point set. The output is a vector layer (polygon geometry) written to the specified destination.

task_name: Create vector grid cells with country intersections
task_description: The script creates a global 2.5°×2.5° regular grid in WGS84 (EPSG:4326), intersects it with Natural Earth's ne_10m_admin_0_countries polygon layer, dissolves resulting fragments by grid cell ID, cleans geometries using GRASS v.clean (tool=10: 'break' at intersections), fixes geometries again, re-dissolves by cell ID, and exports a final shapefile (vcountries.shp) containing only non-overlapping, topologically clean polygons each assigned a unique integer 'cid' field — representing country-portioned grid cells suitable for spatial aggregation or zonal analysis.

task_name: Filter structures near rivers and roads
task_description: The script filters and relocates point-based 'structures' by computing line intersections between 'cours_eau' (rivers) and 'routes' (roads), merging those intersections with the original structures, buffering the merged points by 50 meters, dissolving overlapping buffers, computing centroids of the dissolved polygons, and finally extracting only those centroids within 100 meters of the 'cours_eau' layer. The output is a new point vector layer ('New_structures') containing filtered and spatially adjusted structure locations that are both proximal to road-river intersections and near rivers.

The script locates the N nearest meteorological stations (default N=4) to the centroid of a user-provided basin polygon layer. It computes centroids of the basin, adds an auto-incrementing ID field, performs a distance matrix calculation between the centroid and stations stored at `meteo_stations_path()`, extracts the stations intersecting the distance matrix output, and joins distance attributes back to the station features. The final output is a vector layer of the nearest stations with associated distance metrics.

task_name: Join PtRef with lotic width data
task_description: The script filters point reference features (PtRef) to retain only those whose 'Id_UEA' matches any 'Id_UEA' in the river network layer ('Riv_Net') and where the attribute 'Valide_bv' is true; then joins the filtered points with the 'PtRef_Mod_Lotique' layer on the 'Id_PtRef' field to attach the 'Largeur_mod' (modeled width) attribute. The output is a vector layer ('PtRef_largeur') containing only the matched, validated points enriched with the modeled width value.

The script adapts point-based species occurrence records (e.g., from field surveys or databases) to Maxent-compatible CSV format by: (1) spatially subsetting the input points to only those intersecting a user-provided polygon layer ('Límites de influencia de variables'), (2) optionally dropping specified attribute fields ('Campos de omisión'), and (3) adding X/Y coordinate fields (in project CRS) prefixed with 'Coordenada '. The output is a vector layer with geometry and appended longitude/latitude (or projected X/Y) fields, ready for export to CSV and ingestion by Maxent.

task_name: Split polygon into spatially coherent parts
task_description: The script splits an input polygon feature into a specified number of spatially contiguous sub-polygons using a geometric clustering and partitioning workflow. It first generates random points inside the polygon, applies k-means clustering to group those points into 'numberofparts' clusters, computes concave hulls per cluster to approximate cluster shapes, calculates centroids of those hulls, generates Voronoi polygons from the centroids, and finally intersects the Voronoi tessellation with the original polygon to produce non-overlapping, topology-aware sub-polygons. The output is a vector feature sink ('splittedpolygon') containing the resulting split polygons.

The script generates two shapefile outputs from a NetCDF file: (1) Nc_Grids.shp — a point layer where each point represents the centroid of a NetCDF grid cell, with attributes FGID, Row, Col, Gridlon, Gridlat; and (2) Gridncply.shp — a polygon layer where each polygon approximates the boundary of a NetCDF grid cell using bilinear interpolation of corner coordinates derived from adjacent grid nodes (for rotated grids) or axis-aligned averaging (for non-rotated grids), with identical attributes. It also writes Gridcorr.csv containing the same coordinate/ID table. A second function performs area-weighted spatial overlay between two polygon layers (Target_Ply_Path and Mapping_Ply_Path), producing Overlay_Polygons.shp (the dissolved union geometry with computed area field 's_area') and GriddedForcings2.txt (a text file encoding area-proportional mapping weights from mapping-grid polygons to target-HRU polygons). Both functions rely on QGIS processing algorithms via PyQGIS API and netCDF4 for coordinate extraction.

The script performs geometric operations on surface area polygons stored in a QKan SQLite/SpatiaLite database to resolve overlaps between different surface types (e.g., based on 'abflussparameter'). It creates a temporary table 'temp_flaechencut', computes non-overlapping geometries using ST_Difference and ST_Union, then updates the original 'flaechen' table with cut geometries. Additionally, it generates Voronoi-based catchment areas ('tezg') for selected sewer pipes ('haltungen') by converting pipe centerlines into thin polygons, computing Voronoi skeletons via GRASS v.voronoi.skeleton, clipping to selected subcatchments ('teilgebiete'), and inserting results into the 'tezg' table — all while enforcing topological consistency and validating for intersecting pipes.

The script converts point-based meteorological station time-series data (e.g., TAVG, TMIN, TMAX) into a temporal raster cube — one GeoTIFF per date — using spatial interpolation methods (IDW, nearest neighbor, average, or GWR). It supports log-transformed values, automatic radius estimation, station density filtering, optional clipping to a user-provided vector layer, burning of station values into rasters, and QA reporting. Inputs are fetched via ADSFetchResult (likely from NOAA NCEI’s Applied Climate Data System), with station coordinates derived from metadata or inline LATITUDE/LONGITUDE fields. Outputs include aligned daily/monthly rasters (tif), an optional VRT stack with band names matching dates, COG versions, and a CSV summarizing per-slice station count and statistics (min/max/mean/std). The workflow is CRS-aware, uses GDAL’s gdal.Grid for standard methods and custom NumPy-based GWR for geographically weighted regression, and performs on-the-fly reprojection and extent buffering.

The script performs spatial clipping of QGIS vector and raster layers to a user-defined extent or custom geometry. It processes all visible layers (or all layers if no visibility filter is applied), outputs clipped vector layers (as Shapefile or GeoPackage) and clipped raster layers (as GeoTIFF), preserves WMS/XYZ layer references with extent limiting, reconstructs layer tree groups, map themes, print layouts, and adds a white mask layer covering everything outside the clip area. The final output is a standalone QGIS project (.qgz) containing only the clipped layers, styled identically to originals, centered on the clip extent, and optionally configured to activate a specified map theme on opening. No remote sensing analysis, classification, or time-series processing is performed — it is purely a GIS data subsetting and project packaging tool.

The script computes per-polygon zonal statistics (min, max, sum, count, mean, std, unique, range, var, median, and optionally mode) of raster pixel values intersecting vector polygon features. It reads a user-specified raster band, rasterizes each polygon to a temporary binary mask aligned with the raster grid, applies masking to extract only pixels within the polygon and not equal to the raster's NoData value, and calculates summary statistics on the masked array. The output is a vector layer (same geometry as input) with new attribute fields prefixed by a user-defined string, containing the computed statistics. No specific study area, time range, satellite data, or classification method is embedded — it is a generic GDAL/OGR/QGIS-based raster-vector zonal statistics tool operating on local file paths provided at runtime.

The script computes land use/cover change between two user-provided categorical raster layers (‘before’ and ‘after’) by generating four output rasters: (1) a detailed change raster encoding category transitions as integer values using a positional formula (e.g., ‘after × 10 + before’ for ≤9 categories or ‘after × 1000 + before’ otherwise); (2) a simplified binary raster indicating presence/absence of change (1 = changed, 0 = no change); (3) a gain raster highlighting pixels where a user-specified category appears in the ‘after’ raster but not in the ‘before’ raster; and (4) a loss raster highlighting pixels where the specified category appears in the ‘before’ raster but not in the ‘after’ raster. The script dynamically detects actual category values present in each input raster (not assumed ranges), validates category existence, applies NoData-aware sampling, and auto-generates context-sensitive pseudocolor symbology—including discrete Viridis-based color ramps for the detailed change raster mapping all observed ‘from→to’ transitions. All operations are performed client-side in QGIS using QgsRasterCalculator and QgsRasterShader; no GEE server-side code is present—the script is a QGIS Processing Algorithm, not a Google Earth Engine script. Data sources, study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geographic extent are not specified in the code and are fully user-defined at runtime via input raster layer selection.

The script manages, processes, and visualizes hydrological monitoring data from field-deployed sensors—including flow monitors (FM), depth monitors (DM), pump loggers (PL), and rain gauges (RG)—for wastewater infrastructure surveys. It supports importing raw binary (.dat, .flo) and ASCII (.r, .fdv) time-series data; post-processing raw data into calibrated flow, depth, velocity, and rainfall intensity series; classifying flow data (e.g., dry weather vs. storm); identifying storm events; generating interim reports with plots (FDV, scatter, cumulative depth, DWF, raingauge); producing verification reports against ICM model outputs; and managing GIS-integrated survey projects with site/monitor/installation metadata, photographs, schematics, and spatial coordinates. Outputs include PDF reports (interim summaries, storm event analyses, verification details), CSV exports of processed time-series, and interactive QGIS map layers for flow monitors and rain gauges.

The script computes land cover area statistics (in km²) for user-defined regions (e.g., cities or administrative units) across multiple land cover rasters — initial, final, and intermediate time steps — using zonal statistics. It calculates class-wise area totals per region and time stamp, then visualizes stacked bar charts of land area change alongside a dependent variable (e.g., population or GDP) as a dual-axis plot. It also computes spatial shifts in built-up area centroids over time — both per-region (using vector mask geometries) and globally (across full raster extents) — and visualizes them as labeled point layers and directed line segments on QGIS map canvases with OSM basemap. Outputs include interactive tabbed tables (per region + summary), graphics views (bar charts, centroid trajectories), and exportable PNGs, CSVs, and shapefiles (centroids and shift lines). Input rasters are provided by the user via QGIS layer selectors; no internal GEE asset loading occurs — all raster I/O is local (via rasterio) and vector I/O is via QgsVectorLayer. The script operates entirely within QGIS Python context (PyQt5/QGIS API), not Google Earth Engine — despite the prompt’s mention of 'GEE developer', the code contains zero ee.* imports or GEE calls.

task_name: Validate point location against road buffers
task_description: The script validates the spatial correctness of point features (e.g., roadside markers or infrastructure assets) loaded from a CSV file by checking whether each point falls within a 50-meter buffer around a reference road network layer; it further cross-validates attribute correspondence (via 'cod_strada' field matching between points and road/buffer layers), filters points that satisfy both geometric inclusion and attribute alignment, appends administrative municipality names ('nome' from polygon layer) to validated points via spatial join, and exports the final validated and enriched point set as both a Shapefile and a CSV with XYZ geometry coordinates.

task_name: Visualize hurricane wind field and track
task_description: The script generates a static PNG/JPEG layout map from a QGIS project that overlays a hurricane wind field raster (PNG) and a hurricane track vector layer (CSV) onto a base map. The hurricane wind field is styled using a categorized QML style ('hurricane_cat_raster.qml'), and the track is styled with a line-based QML ('hurricane_track.qml'). The layout extent is automatically set to the bounding box of the non-base-map layer (i.e., raster or track), reprojected from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to Web Mercator (EPSG:3857). Legend items are customized: the raster layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Wind Field" and its legend node order is fixed to indices [2–7]; the track layer is renamed to "[HurricaneName] [Year] Track" (if forecasts excluded) and its legend node order set to [0]; the base map layer is removed from the legend. The final output is a cropped, timestamped JPEG file (e.g., 'larry2021_100x100_2023-10-05T142000Z.jpeg') saved in the data directory. Input data paths are derived from a hurricane file base string (e.g., 'LARRY_2021_100x100'), implying hurricane name, year, and spatial resolution — but no geospatial processing (e.g., reprojection, resampling, classification) is performed in this script; it is purely cartographic export using precomputed raster and vector assets. Study area and time range are not specified in the code — only hurricane metadata (name/year/resolution) is parsed from the input string.

task_name: Reproject future climate and land cover rasters
task_description: The script reprojects two sets of raster datasets to EPSG:4326 with 0.01° resolution: (1) ensemble bioclimatic rasters for the future climate scenario 'ssp585_2071_2100' (8-GCM ensemble, BioClim variables), stored under '/Users/huangliting/Desktop/kissing_bugs_stats/future_reprojection/ssp585_2071_2100/'; and (2) seven land-cover class rasters (water, forest, grassland, barren, cropland, urban, permanent_snow_ice) extracted from a multi-band global LULC dataset under SSP1-RCP26 for 2025, reprojected and stored under '/Users/huangliting/Desktop/kissing_bugs_stats/future_reprojection/global_SSP1_RCP26_2025/'. No classification or modeling is performed—the script is purely geoprocessing: band extraction, reprojection, and resampling using QGIS GDAL warp and raster calculator.

The script tiles an input raster layer into user-defined polygon tiles from a vector tiling scheme layer. It first warps the source raster to match the tiling scheme’s CRS and spatial extent (using GDAL Warp), then computes a bounding polygon of the warped raster, and finally extracts each intersecting tile using GDAL Translate with projWin. For existing tile files, it performs pixel-wise update (non-overwrite: new pixels replace nodata in existing tiles). Outputs are GeoTIFF tiles organized in subfolders named after tile attributes, with preserved metadata and band names. No study area, time range, satellite data, or classification methods are involved — this is a pure geospatial data structuring/management operation on arbitrary raster inputs.

The script validates that QGIS has correctly installed and configured external geoprocessing dependencies: SAGA GIS (version 2.3.x), GRASS GIS, core plugins ('processing', 'MetaSearch', 'db_manager'), ESRI File Geodatabase (GDB) driver support, GeoPackage (GPKG) read/write capability, and GDAL raster processing algorithms (e.g., 'gdal:rastercalculator'). It does this by programmatically checking version strings, folder configurations, plugin activation status, layer validity for sample GDB and GPKG files, and successful execution of a GDAL raster calculation. No geospatial analysis, modeling, or mapping is performed; outputs are boolean test results and temporary file existence checks.

The script reclassifies all GeoTIFF files in a local directory into four discrete classes based on pixel value thresholds (1: <100, 2: 100–499, 3: 500–999, 4: ≥1000) using QGIS Raster Calculator. It processes each .tif file sequentially, reads it as a QgsRasterLayer, defines a band-1 arithmetic expression, and writes the output as a new GeoTIFF in a locally created 'RESULTADOS_CALCULADORA' subfolder. No remote sensing data sources, cloud masking, temporal filtering, or geographic projection handling is present — inputs are arbitrary local rasters with no metadata constraints. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and coordinate system are not specified in the script.

The script converts a vector polygon layer (with an 'ID' attribute) into a raster grid matching the geometry (columns, rows, geotransform, projection) of an input raster. It uses GDAL's RasterizeLayer to burn the 'ID' field values into the output raster, with NoData set to 0 and background filled with 0. The workflow includes saving the input vector layer to a temporary Shapefile, opening it via OGR, and writing the result to a temporary GeoTIFF. No classification, time-series analysis, or satellite-derived computation is performed — this is purely a vector-to-raster conversion utility function operating on pre-existing local raster and vector inputs. All parameters (crs, cols, rows, geotransform) are passed in; no study area, time range, or remote sensing data sources are referenced or inferred from the code.

task_name: Extract OpenStreetMap patches for urban areas
task_description: The script extracts georeferenced 256×256 PNG patches of OpenStreetMap (OSM) basemap imagery and co-located Sentinel-2 spectral band composites (B4, B3, B2, B8) over user-defined geographic regions. It operates by subdividing a Sentinel-2 tile’s spatial extent into regular or overlapped grid patches (based on a user-provided example patch extent in EPSG:3857), then exporting OSM tiles via QGIS layout export at zoom level ~14–17 (adjusted via tile_size scaling factor /8 * 1.5). For each patch, it exports an OSM RGB image and — via `layoutbased_extract_raster_portion` — extracts corresponding Sentinel-2 JP2 band files (B4/B3/B2/B8) using QGIS layout-based raster clipping. The workflow is explicitly tied to predefined cities (‘Paris’, ‘Madrid’, ‘Toulouse’, ‘Poitiers’) and uses Sentinel-2 tile IDs (e.g., ‘T30TVK’) and file paths pointing to local JP2 assets. Outputs include: (1) PNG files named as ‘patch_{tile_id}_{x:03}_{y:03}_OSM.png’, (2) NumPy `.npz` files storing the bounding box extents of all generated patches (e.g., ‘np_extent_T30TVK_EPSG_3857.npz’), and (3) implicitly, co-registered Sentinel-2 band patches (though the band extraction function lacks explicit band selection logic and assumes full JP2 file input). The study area is limited to urban subregions within these four European cities; no temporal filtering or time-series analysis is performed — only static snapshot extraction. Data sources are local Sentinel-2 JP2 files and remote OSM XYZ tiles.

task_name: Calculate spectral vegetation and environmental indices
task_description: The script calculates 10 spectral indices (ARVI, BRI, CVI, GCI, NBRI, GVMI, NDSI, NDVI, SAVI, SIPI) from user-selected raster layers loaded in QGIS. It uses QGIS's QgsRasterCalculator to perform band arithmetic on Sentinel-2–compatible bands (e.g., blue, green, red, VNIR, NIR, B9, B11, B12), implying input rasters correspond to Sentinel-2 Level-1C or Level-2A products. The workflow requires manual selection of raster layers for each band via dropdowns in a QGIS plugin dialog; no automatic data ingestion, cloud masking, temporal aggregation, or spatial subsetting is performed. Outputs are GeoTIFF files (e.g., 'ndvi.tif', 'gvmi.tif') written to a user-specified folder and optionally loaded into the QGIS map canvas. No study area, time range, or coordinate system is programmatically defined — all geospatial inputs are assumed pre-loaded and aligned by the user. Band assignments follow standard Sentinel-2 spectral definitions: B02=blue, B03=green, B04=red, B05=VNIR (red edge 1), B08=NIR, B09=water vapor, B11=SWIR-1, B12=SWIR-2.

The script prepares input data for an LUHI (Local Urban Heat Island) analysis by ingesting and organizing geospatial rasters including Landsat 9 LST (Land Surface Temperature), DEM, land cover (DWV1), soil texture, canopy height, hydrologic soil group, and LCZ (Local Climate Zone) layers. It extracts EPSG from the Landsat filename to auto-generate standardized output filenames (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif'), reorganizes input files into 'Data' and 'Results' subfolders, sets the calculation extent by reprojecting the Landsat raster’s bounding box to EPSG:4326, and collects user-defined field names for attribute mapping. The final output is a parameter dictionary passed to ExtractionDuFichierCsvPourOutilIa — an algorithm that converts these rasters into a CSV table for downstream IA (AI/ML) tool use. No time-series or temporal aggregation is performed; the Landsat 9 image is treated as a single static snapshot. Study area is inferred from folder naming ('city' extracted from parent directory name, e.g., 'Paris_2023_32632'), but no explicit city or region is hardcoded. Data sources are all local file paths (not GEE asset IDs), so satellite metadata is derived only from filename conventions (e.g., 'LST_32632.tif') and UI labels ('Image LandSat 9').

The script computes water indices (NDVI and NDWI2) from multiband raster inputs, applies thresholding to generate binary water/non-water masks, filters small objects using morphological regularization (OTB) or sieve filtering (GDAL), and vectorizes the final raster mask into polygons. It supports both OTB and QGIS-native processing backends. Inputs are local raster files (e.g., GeoTIFF) with at least 4 bands; band mapping is configured via a dictionary (conf.channelOrderDic) specifying 'Red', 'Green', and 'NIR' channels. The workflow is fully local — no Earth Engine server-side computation — and targets operational cartographic production of water bodies ('Cart'Eau' plugin by Cerema). No satellite collection, time series, or cloud masking is involved; all operations are single-scene, user-provided rasters. Study area, time range, and sensor metadata are not embedded in the code and must be supplied externally via file paths and configuration.

The script implements a QGIS plugin for real-time GPS field data collection, logging, and visualization. It connects to GPS hardware via serial ports, acquires WGS84 coordinates (latitude/longitude), elevation, and direction; transforms coordinates between CRSs (e.g., WGS84 ↔ PUWG 1992/EPSG:2180); supports manual point capture, interval-based automatic sampling, resection (two-point intersection), offset measurement (perpendicular offset from bearing), and group-enclave management. Outputs include an in-memory point list with attributes (x, y, lp, text, group_id, checked), on-canvas markers and paths, optional NMEA log files, and exportable vector features to QGIS layers. No satellite, remote sensing, or time-series analysis is performed — all operations are client-side, real-time, and sensor-agnostic (hardware GPS only). Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external geospatial datasets are not specified.

task_name: Infer tree canopy height and bounding boxes
task_description: The script performs inference on an input raster layer using one of four deep learning models (HighResCanopyHeight, Mask R-CNN, DeepForest, or VHRTrees) to generate either: (1) a grayscale GeoTIFF raster representing canopy height (HighResCanopyHeight), (2) a binary GeoTIFF raster (Mask R-CNN), or (3) a vector ESRI Shapefile containing bounding boxes around individual trees (DeepForest and VHRTrees). Input is a user-provided local raster layer (e.g., 'HSJ_4_77') whose path is obtained via QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().dataSourceUri(); the layer’s extent is transformed to EPSG:4326 for geospatial consistency. Model weights are loaded from a user-configured directory stored in QGIS settings under 'TreeEyed/modelDir'. No satellite imagery, cloud masking, temporal filtering, or spectral index computation is performed — the script is purely a local, model-driven inference wrapper that consumes a preloaded raster and outputs either raster or vector results based on model selection. Study area, time range, sensor, bands, and satellite are not specified in the code — only the raster’s CRS and extent are used for coordinate handling.

The script enables interactive selection, buffering, merging, and copying of vector features from user-selected layers into a temporary 'Vector Mosaic' scratch layer (EPSG:27700). It supports point-click selection, rectangular area selection, disc/buffer creation (with optional curve geometry), feature removal by click, merging of selected geometries into a single multipart feature, copying to clipboard, and clearing the mosaic. Style attributes (fill and stroke colors) are extracted from the source layer’s renderer (categorized or single-symbol) and stored as CSV-encoded RGBA strings in the mosaic layer’s 'Fill' and 'Border' fields. No remote sensing data processing, raster analysis, or time-series operations occur — it is purely a QGIS desktop plugin for vector feature curation and composition.

The script generates vector contour layers (isochrones) representing fire arrival time intervals from Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) output files. It parses the CHID.out file to extract geographic origin (latitude/longitude), transforms it to the user-specified CRS, reads FDS boundary file (BNDF) data for 'FIRE ARRIVAL TIME', applies a fixed threshold of 0, and produces time-contoured polygons at user-defined t_step (seconds) intervals. Outputs include a classified QgsVectorLayer with 'time' attribute, symbolized using graduated Magma color ramp; no raster or satellite data is used — inputs are local FDS simulation outputs (e.g., CHID.out, CHID_*.bnf). Study area, time range, and sensor/band information are not specified in the code.

task_name: Identify connected line features with matching attributes
task_description: The script analyzes a vector line layer to detect topologically connected line segments (i.e., lines sharing endpoints or intersecting at points) and checks whether those connected features share identical values across user-specified attribute fields. It outputs a point layer where each point represents an intersection location between two connected lines, annotated with a 'flag' string identifying the pair of feature IDs and stating that they are connected and have identical attribute values. The algorithm uses QgsSpatialIndex for spatial proximity acceleration, computes intersections via QgsGeometry.intersection(), filters self-comparisons, avoids duplicate points using geometry equality checks, and applies strict attribute value comparison (not tolerance-based or type-coerced). No raster data, time series, or external geospatial datasets are involved — input is purely a local QGIS vector layer of type LineString; study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and external data sources are not specified.

The script provides a comprehensive set of utility functions for interacting with QgsVectorLayer objects in QGIS, including listing layers by geometry type or provider, checking projection status, retrieving field names and types, validating field content (nulls, uniqueness, numeric validity), extracting attribute values (with/without nulls, selected features only), identifying ID fields, adding new fields, creating temporary memory layers from tabular data, building spatial indexes, and constructing topological link lists from line layers. It does not perform remote sensing analysis, image processing, or Earth Engine (GEE) operations — despite the prompt’s reference to 'GEE script', this is purely a QGIS Python plugin/module for desktop GIS vector data management and preprocessing. No satellite imagery, time-series, classification, or geospatial modeling is implemented or invoked.

The script merges line features (e.g., stream networks, road segments, or drainage lines) that touch at endpoints and share compatible directions within a user-defined angular tolerance (0–90°). It operates on vector line layers in QGIS Processing Framework (not GEE — despite the prompt’s mischaracterization), computing azimuths of start/end segments to evaluate directional alignment. Two attribute handling modes are supported: (1) merging only lines with identical attributes, or (2) preserving attributes of the longer line after merging. Linear rings (closed lines) are excluded from merging and passed through unchanged. Outputs are a new vector layer of merged polylines with updated geometries and attributes. No satellite, temporal, or geographic metadata is embedded — it is a generic, location- and time-agnostic vector processing algorithm.

The script processes vector-based hydrographic data (e.g., drainage networks or basin boundaries) stored in ESRI Shapefile format to decompose multipart geometries (MultiLineString, MultiPolygon), extract vertices and ordered line segments, compute topological attributes (Strahler order, Shreve order, Sharp index), and export a restructured Shapefile with enhanced hydrological attributes and cartographic styling. It handles geometry orientation (flow direction), detects multipart features and splits them into individual features with observational metadata, applies rule-based labeling (Sharp and Shreve values along lines), and sets dynamic symbology (e.g., stroke width scaled by Strahler order, color based on Sharp presence). The output is a styled QGIS vector layer added to the current project, with auxiliary files (.prj, .shx, etc.) copied; no raster, satellite, or time-series data is involved — input is purely static vector hydrography.

The script creates multiple polygon buffers at user-specified distances around input vector features (e.g., points, lines, or polygons). It computes successive Euclidean distance buffers using QgsGeometry.buffer() with 24 quadrant segments, and optionally computes ring-shaped annuli by differencing consecutive buffers when 'Outside Polygons Only' is enabled. Each output feature retains the original attributes plus a new 'rind_dist' field indicating its buffer distance. The output is a single vector polygon layer with one feature per ring per input feature. No raster data, time-series, satellite imagery, or classification is involved — it is a pure vector geoprocessing operation in QGIS Processing Framework.

The script queries a PostgreSQL/SpatiaLite database to retrieve Landsat catalog records (image ID, path/row, acquisition date, orbit, point, geometry) that spatially intersect a specified Brazilian municipality (geocoded as '1304104', corresponding to Manaus, Amazonas). It uses an SQL JOIN with the 'municipio_ibge' administrative boundary layer and applies MbrIntersects and ST_Intersects for spatial filtering. The output is a QGIS vector layer named 'landsat_muni_1304104' containing matching Landsat scenes, styled using either a local QML file or a database-stored QML style, and added to the QGIS map canvas with a temporary red highlight polygon around the input municipality geometry. No Earth Engine (GEE) processing occurs — this is purely a QGIS Python plugin-style database query and layer loading workflow.

The script generates ADHydro-compatible meteorological forcing files (specifically precipitation rate in m/s and other variables like temperature, humidity, wind, radiation) by spatially intersecting AORC (Atmospheric/Oceanic Regional Climate Model) gridded data with ADHydro hydrologic mesh and channel elements. It reads hourly AORC netCDF files (e.g., 'AORC_Charlotte_YYYYMMDDHH.nc4') and higher-resolution MRMS-disaggregated 15-minute precip files ('AORC_MRMS_Charlotte_YYYYMMDDHHMM.nc') from a local directory structure organized by year. It performs geometric intersection using QGIS spatial indexing and Shapely geometry operations to map each ADHydro element (polygon or line) to the best-fitting AORC grid cell — either by centroid containment or by largest area/length intersection. Precipitation is converted from accumulated mass (kg/m²) to rate (m/s) using water density (temperature-dependent rho function) and time intervals derived from adjacent timestamps. Outputs include time-series forcing arrays for mesh and channel elements, domain-level mass balance diagnostics (saved to 'domain_precip_rates.csv'), and diagnostic plots. The study area is implicitly defined by a shapefile 'sub9_catchment.shp' projected into ADHydro sinusoidal coordinates; the script processes only AORC cells intersecting this sub-basin, identified via geopandas overlay and percent-intersection calculation.

The script converts a vector line layer into a multiline layer by grouping topologically connected (touching or intersecting) line features into single multilinestring geometries. It uses a spatial index for efficient candidate search and Union-Find with path compression and union-by-rank to identify connected components. Each output feature is a QgsMultiLineString composed of all line parts from its connected component, with an attribute 'length' storing the total geometric length. No remote sensing data, time series, or raster operations are involved — it is a pure vector geometric aggregation algorithm operating on input vector features in their native CRS. Study area, time range, satellite data, bands, and external datasets are not specified.

The script visualizes and manages polygon-based agricultural 'Komplex' (complex) units in a GIS interface, derived from relational database entities (BKomplex, BKomplexName, BKoppel) and their associated geometries. It constructs vector layers in EPSG:31259 by aggregating (combining) geometries from related 'Koppel' (field parcel) records via spatial union operations. Attributes include complex ID, number, and name; geometry is computed from WKT representations of database-stored geometries using geoalchemy2 and QgsGeometry. The output is a styled QGIS memory vector layer ('Komplexe') with red symbology ('komplex_rot'), displayed in a table-and-map view, supporting filtering, sorting (by 'komplex_nr'), and deletion workflows. No remote sensing or satellite-derived analysis is performed — all data originates from internal PostgreSQL/PostGIS database tables and is rendered client-side in QGIS. Study area and time range are not encoded in the script.

The script exports selected QGIS vector layers to KML format, reprojecting them to WGS84 (EPSG:4326). It does not perform any remote sensing analysis, classification, or geoprocessing — it is a pure export utility. The workflow involves listing loaded vector layers in the QGIS project, allowing user selection via a Qt list view, prompting for a save directory, and writing each selected layer as a KML file using QgsVectorFileWriter with UTF-8 encoding and CRS 4326. No satellite data, time series, spectral indices, or thematic modeling is involved; the input layers originate from the local QGIS project and are unspecified in source, extent, or content.

The script reads a spreadsheet (predio.xlsx) containing point coordinates (X,Y), constructs a Point geometry for each row, creates a Polygon from those points to represent a property boundary, computes its area, generates a minimum bounding circle buffered by 20 units, expands the bounding rectangle by 50 units in x-direction, and outputs three shapefiles: the original polygon ('predio1.shp'), the expanded rectangular frame ('marco1.shp'), and the input vertices as points ('vertices.shp'). It then loads all three layers into the current QGIS project. The CRS is explicitly set to EPSG:4486 (SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic).

The script exports a QGIS vector layer to a file in CSV or GeoPackage format, using QgsVectorFileWriter.writeAsVectorFormatV2. It supports automatic filename incrementing on collision and writes geometry as WKT for CSV. The output is the file path of the successfully written vector file or None if write fails.

The script generates a CHANBANK.DAT text file that pairs grid cell IDs (from a 'grid' layer) intersecting the left bank geometry with those intersecting the right bank geometry, based on centroid intersection. It processes vector layers ('user_left_bank', 'user_right_bank', and 'grid') loaded from a GeoPackage, uses spatial indexing for efficient bounding-box–based candidate retrieval, then performs precise geometry–centroid intersection tests. The output is a line-delimited list of space-separated left-grid-fid right-grid-fid pairs, intended for FLO-2D hydraulic modeling input. Study area is inferred as Lake Havasu (from path), but no time range, satellite data, or remote sensing operations are present — all inputs are static local vector layers; no imagery, bands, sensors, or temporal filtering is used.

task_name: Calculate pastoral estate burnt percentage by district
task_description: The script calculates the percentage of pastoral estate area burnt by fire within specific administrative districts in southern Northern Territory, Australia. It retrieves district-specific pastoral property boundaries from a QGIS layer, unions their geometries, computes total district estate area and intersected fire-scar area (using a pre-dissolved fire scar geometry), converts areas from m² to km², and writes district name, total estate area (km²), burnt estate area (km²), and percentage burnt to a CSV file. The output is a tabular summary for four districts: Tennant Creek, Northern Alice Springs, Plenty, and Southern Alice Springs.

The script exports a local ESRI Shapefile of buildings ("/qgis_data/shapes/building.shp") to GeoJSON format, reprojects it to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and uploads it to geojson.io via a GitHub Gist URL. The output is a web-accessible interactive map link opened in the default system browser. No remote GEE data, satellite imagery, time-series analysis, classification, or geospatial modeling is performed—the workflow is purely local QGIS vector layer export and web sharing. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor/bands, and geospatial operations beyond reprojection and format conversion are not specified.

task_name: Calculate intervisibility between turbines and houses
task_description: The script computes viewshed-based intervisibility from individual wind turbines to nearby housing points within a 15 km buffer, using a pre-generated VRT DEM raster and QGIS-based viewshed analysis. It loads turbine and housing point layers, buffers each turbine, spatially subsets houses within each buffer, runs a custom viewshed calculation (via doViewshedHack) to determine line-of-sight visibility, and appends property title numbers from the housing layer to the resulting intervisibility vector output. Outputs include per-turbine intervisibility shapefiles with fields: Source, Target, Visible, TargetSize, Distance, and TitleNo.

The script tests QgsMapLayerUtils.combinedExtent() to compute the bounding box encompassing multiple QGIS map layers (vector, raster, annotation, group) in specified CRS, verifying correct coordinate transformation and extent union behavior. It also tests layer source matching, source path updating, layer type sorting, and layer name laundering functionality.

The script generates PDF reports (synthesis, map, and vertices) for cadastral parcels ('logradouro' features) by analyzing spatial overlaps with reference layers (e.g., 'Área Homologada', SHP/WFS/DB layers). It creates memory-based intersection layers (point/line/polygon) filtered per parcel and layer name, computes overlap area/length using CRS-specific geometry calculations, inserts dynamic text (headers, data sources, overlay status), exports atlas-driven layouts (A3 landscape map, A4 portrait synthesis), merges PDFs per parcel, and cleans intermediate layers. Outputs are time-stamped, parcel-named PDFs containing cartographic maps, textual summaries of overlaps, and metadata on data provenance.

The script classifies LiDAR-derived forest stand types (e.g., 'Clara', 'Regeneracion', 'Resalveo', and 30+ coded mass types like 'Monte Bravo', 'Latizal', 'Fustal') using metrics derived from LAS/LAZ point clouds: fractional canopy cover (fcc), height of canopy (hm), height of base of canopy (hbc), crown ratio (rc), and projected growth-adjusted versions. It applies rule-based raster algebra with user-defined thresholds (e.g., fccalta=95.0, hclaras=12.0) to assign categorical codes, vectorizes the result, filters by area (>2500 m²), and applies thematic symbology. Outputs include merged shapefiles for 'Clara_merged', 'Regeneracion_merged', 'Resalveo_merged', and 'Teselas_merged' with categorized rendering based on DN values and a predefined color/label lookup table.

The script models passive margin wedge (PMW) geometry and sediment thickness along profiles derived from multi-point features representing passive margins. It computes crest positions (X_CREST, Z_CREST), raster-sampled bathymetry (Z_RASTER), wedge extent (X_MAX), and integrates abyssal sediment thickness and density to derive node-level properties (Z_WITH_SED, H_SED, RHO_SED) for each point along PMW profiles. Inputs include age-dependent parametric passive margin models (PMConversionTools), raster-derived depth (qgis_tin_raster_prelim_*.tif), continent polygon boundaries, and sediment property functions (SEDConversionTools). Outputs are GeoJSON files: PMW_profiles_*.geojson (multi-point profile geometries) and PMW_nodes_*.geojson (point features with geophysical attributes per age slice).

The script performs automated pebble (gravel-sized sediment) detection on georeferenced aerial or drone imagery using Mask R-CNN. It accepts an input raster image, a scale line vector layer and its known physical length to compute ground resolution, applies georeferencing and scaling to the image, tiles it with configurable overlap, sends each tile to a remote inference server running a custom-trained Mask R-CNN model (via socket communication), converts resulting binary masks into vector polygon contours, filters overlapping detections using IoU-based merging, computes approximate grain length from polygon geometry, and outputs a MultiPolygon vector layer of pebble contours with 'Len' attribute. The workflow relies on rasterio for mask-to-vector conversion, OpenCV for resizing, GDAL for geotransform manipulation, and QGIS Processing Framework for integration.

The script generates a digital elevation model (DEM) for stable beach areas by extracting elevation profiles along two parallel shore-normal lines (Line A and Line B) from an input DEM layer, applying a slope constraint to define the beach face, and optionally interpolating a smoothed surface using inverse distance weighting (IDW) or similar methods (mode='wmean'). It also generates cross-shore elevation profiles as a vector layer. The outputs include: (1) a GeoTIFF DEM raster at user-specified output path; (2) optionally, an interpolated surface raster (_surface.tif); (3) optionally, a cropped version of that surface using a mask polygon layer (_mask.shp); and (4) a vector layer of elevation profiles (_profiles.shp). All outputs are automatically loaded into QGIS. Input data sources are local QGIS layers — no remote Earth Engine datasets are used; the script operates entirely within QGIS using its native raster/vector processing capabilities.

The script generates a multi-criteria land suitability map by loading and styling two raster layers — a base map and a final suitability raster — then composing them into a publication-ready PDF layout in QGIS. It applies custom symbology (via .qml), adjusts map extent with a vertical offset (+2200 y-units), adds title, north arrow, scale bar in kilometers, and a cleaned legend showing '1.0 (High)' to '0.0 (Low)' suitability scores. The output is a PDF file named 'mapa_entregable_final_km_v13.pdf' containing the styled map layout.

task_name: Extract line length and elevation endpoints
task_description: The script processes a line shapefile and a raster DEM to compute the length of each line feature, transform its start and end points to the raster's CRS, and sample elevation values at those transformed points. It outputs a text file containing for each line (or each part of a MultiLineString): length (rounded to 2 decimals), transformed start/end coordinates (x/y), and corresponding sampled elevation values from the raster. The workflow uses QgsVectorLayer and QgsRasterLayer, coordinate transformation via QgsCoordinateTransform, and raster sampling via dataProvider().sample().

task_name: Tile raster and vector data into patches
task_description: The script tiles a georeferenced TIFF raster into overlapping rectangular patches using a grid generated from the raster's extent and resolution, optionally clips each patch using a buffered shapefile of ground truth features (e.g., nests), and exports both tiled rasters and corresponding YOLO-formatted bounding box annotations (class '0') derived from intersections between buffered features and each patch. Key operations include GDAL warp reprojection, QGIS grid creation, vector buffering, raster clipping by mask, and geometric intersection-based annotation extraction.

task_name: Derive salinity indices from Landsat bands
task_description: The script computes 10 spectral indices (SI1–SI10) from Landsat Band 2 (blue), Band 3 (green), Band 4 (red), and Band 5 (NIR) to serve as proxies for sea surface salinity (SSS), using raster algebra in QGIS. It then samples these indices against SSS values extracted from SMAP-derived NetCDF files (via VRT/XYZ conversion), merges the sampled results into a unified CSV per scene with longitude, latitude, SSS, and all 10 SI values, and exports them to 'C:/Users/MLMan/Desktop/CSVs/'. The workflow is fully local-file-based, operating on pre-downloaded Landsat Level-1 or TOA imagery and co-located SMAP SSS NetCDF products.

The script implements a multi-exposure impact analysis framework that concurrently processes ≥2 exposure layers (e.g., population, buildings, roads) with a single hazard layer (e.g., flood, earthquake) and an optional aggregation layer (e.g., administrative boundaries). It orchestrates multiple individual ImpactFunction instances—one per exposure—then synthesizes results into two core output layers: (1) a multi-exposure aggregation summary layer (vector polygon), aggregating impact counts per aggregation unit across all exposures; and (2) a multi-exposure analysis summary layer (vector polygon), representing the union of analysis extents and containing exposure-specific impact statistics. Provenance metadata is rigorously tracked for all inputs (hazard, exposures, aggregation), CRS, analysis extent, datastore URI, and output layers. The workflow includes input validation, CRS/extent consistency checks, layer cloning, parallel IF execution, geometric union of extents, and GIS operations including vector preparation, virtual aggregation creation, and summary statistics computation via safe.gis.vector.summary_5_multi_exposure functions. No satellite imagery, time-series, or pixel-based remote sensing operations are performed—the script operates entirely on preloaded QGIS vector/raster map layers within the InaSAFE desktop or Celery environment. Study area, time range, and sensor/band details are not specified in the code.

task_name: Manage FLO-2D geopackage schema and data
task_description: The script implements comprehensive GeoPackage (GPKG) database utilities for the FLO-2D hydraulic modeling plugin in QGIS. It handles geopackage creation, connection/disconnection, metadata and parameter management (via `cont` and `metadata` tables), spatial geometry operations (centroid extraction, buffer, linestring/multilinestring/polygon construction, grid cell queries), table schema validation and migration, QGZ project synchronization (including XML-level path correction and hex-encoded binary round-trip), vector/raster layer import from external GPKGs, infiltration area mapping, channel schematization (right bank lines, interior node polygonization), and automated population of default values (e.g., reservoir names, Manning’s n). Key workflows include `copy_from_other()` for version-upgrading geopackages, `check_qgis_project()` for runtime QGZ consistency, and `update_layer_extents()` for spatial metadata compliance.

task_name: Validate radar precipitation against gauge measurements
task_description: The script validates 15-minute rainfall estimates from radar imagery against in-situ rain gauge measurements in the Yom River basin, Thailand. It reads gauge station metadata (including WGS84 coordinates) and time-synchronized 15-minute gauge rainfall values from CSV files; transforms station coordinates from WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647); samples radar raster values at each transformed gauge location using QgsRasterLayer.dataProvider().sample(); and writes paired gauge-radar rainfall values (station ID, gauge mm, radar mm) to a CSV file ('temp_val15min.csv') for statistical validation. The study area is the Yom River basin; the time is fixed to a single timestamp — 2018-07-17 at 18:00 (15-minute accumulation); data sources are local CSV files (gauge locations and 15-min rainfall) and a local GeoTIFF radar mosaic (path_rr); no satellite or sensor is involved — the radar data is ground-based (weather radar), not satellite-derived; geospatial operations include coordinate transformation and point sampling; output is a CSV table of collocated gauge-radar pairs.

task_name: Convert valid pixel count to binary mask
task_description: The script processes GeoTIFF raster files representing 'valid pixel count' (likely derived from tree cover or similar land cover metrics) by applying a threshold-based binary classification: pixels with value > 0 are assigned 1, others 0. It uses QGIS’s QgsRasterCalculator with expression '(raster@1 > 0) * 1' to generate new GeoTIFFs prefixed with 'gt0_'. Input rasters are read from a local Windows path containing no embedded geospatial metadata about study area, time, or sensor — all processing is purely local raster algebra on precomputed datasets. No satellite imagery, time-series filtering, cloud masking, or spectral band operations occur in the script; it operates solely on existing single-band rasters. Output is a set of binary rasters indicating presence/absence of valid pixels, saved to a local output folder. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and bands are not specified in the code.

The script computes population-weighted population density (popop) by performing zonal statistics on administrative polygons (world_geolev1_2019.shp) using two LandScan raster layers: pop_robinson.tif (population) and pop2_robinson.tif (population squared). It calculates the mean of each raster within each polygon, then derives popop as the ratio of pop2_mean to pop_mean. The output is a CSV file (popop_geolev1.csv) containing polygon attributes plus the two zonal means, intended for post-processing to compute the final popop ratio.

The script implements a QGIS plugin that adds interactive web map layers (e.g., Google Maps, Bing Maps, OpenStreetMap, Stamen, MapQuest, Apple Maps, and Buenos Aires-specific historical aerial imagery) to QGIS via the OpenLayers JavaScript API or GDAL TMS raster layers. It registers layer types, manages CRS transformation for proper alignment, handles proxy configuration for HTTP requests, supports API key entry for Google Maps, and provides an overview panel and about dialog. Outputs include dynamically loaded basemap layers in QGIS with appropriate coordinate reference system handling and user-facing UI elements (menu, dialogs, message bar notifications).

The script computes a spatially explicit, normalized, and weighted overlay risk map by integrating multiple user-provided geospatial risk factor layers (vector or raster) within a defined study area. Each factor is processed through proximity conversion (if vector), min-max normalization to [0,1], optional inversion for inverse-risk correlation ('Lower values = Higher Risk'), and then combined via weighted linear combination. The final output is a clipped raster risk map (0–1 scale) named '{project_name}_RiskMap_Clipped.tif', loaded into the QGIS project.

The script generates WMS-based raster layers for elevation slices (kote) or digital height models (dhm) from a geospatial web service, using user-selected model ID, slice type (e.g., 'slice_kote' or 'slice_dhm'), and depth/level parameter. It constructs a custom WMS URI with EPSG:25832 CRS, PNG format, and dynamic viewparams (model ID and level/depth), adds the layer to QGIS, sets opacity to 0.6, and updates layer naming based on model name and depth/level. The tool interacts with a backend slice service via authenticated HTTP requests (using API key) and dynamically selects the highest-priority geospatial model intersecting the map canvas center.

The script computes a weighted raster-based propagation index using five clipped input rasters: 'uso_solo_clipped' (land use/cover), 'clinografia_clipped' (slope), 'orientacao_vertente_clipped' (aspect), 'rodovia_clipped' (road proximity), and 'hipsom_clipped' (elevation). It constructs a QgsRasterCalculator expression '1 + (100 * "v") + (30 * "s") + (10 * "a") + (5 * "r") + (2 * "e")', where each variable maps to a band-1 reference of the respective layer. The calculation is executed over the extent, width, and height of the first layer ('uso_solo_clipped'), outputting a single GeoTIFF file at 'D:\Projetos\0023.2016_TAESA\data\propagacao\tmp\propagacao_19.tif'. The result code is interpreted using a predefined message list to report success or failure.

The script performs a raster-based elevation threshold operation on a DSM (Digital Surface Model) file, specifically extracting pixels where elevation values exceed 2000 meters. It uses QGIS's QgsRasterCalculator to evaluate the expression 'D46521204_0101_DSMFirst.asc@1 > 2000' and exports the binary result (1 for true, 0 for false) as a GeoTIFF ('C:/Users/roberta/Desktop/testchm2.tif'). The input DSM is explicitly sourced from a local file path containing 'DSM_CORTINA_2010_CONTRATTO_140', indicating the Cortina d'Ampezzo area in the Italian Dolomites; no DTM is actually used in the calculation despite being defined in commented-out code. The workflow is purely pixel-wise logical evaluation — no classification model, no time-series, no multispectral bands, no cloud masking or compositing. Output is a single-band binary raster representing high-elevation areas (>2000 m) within the DSM extent.

The script generates a vector grid (points, lines, rectangles, diamonds, or hexagons) aligned to a geographic coordinate system (EPSG:4326) using user-defined scale-based spacing (e.g., 0.025° for 1:25k), derived from the bounding box of an input vector layer. It optionally separates vertical and horizontal grid lines, adds a 'ROTULO' field containing rounded longitude values (for points/lines), and outputs the grid as one or more vector layers (full grid, vertical lines, horizontal lines) in the specified target CRS.

task_name: Load Queensland property and geoscience boundaries
task_description: The script loads vector layers representing property boundaries (Lot/Plan parcels), tenure data, and geology layers (detailed 1:100k and regional 1:500k/1:1M) from Queensland Government feature services. It parses user-provided Lot/Plan identifiers (e.g., '53SP253460'), retrieves corresponding property polygons via a cadastre service, reprojects them to GDA2020 (EPSG:7844), adds them to the QGIS project, zooms the canvas to their extent, and optionally loads associated tenure and geology layers from REST feature services. Outputs include vector layers saved to a user-specified directory with QML styling; no raster data, classification, or time-series analysis is performed. Data sources are Queensland Government-hosted feature services under 'PlanningCadastre', 'LandParcelPropertyFramework', 'GeoscientificInformation/GeologyDetailed', and 'GeoscientificInformation/GeologyRegional'.

task_name: Download and process GHSL settlement data
task_description: The script downloads Global Human Settlements Layer (GHSL) data for a specified extent in Mollweide projection (ESRI:54009), transforms the extent to WGS84 (EPSG:4326), retrieves intersecting GHSL tiles, downloads and unpacks them, reclassifies raster values, polygonizes the reclassified rasters, and merges the resulting vector layers into a single GeoParquet file (ghsl_{filename}.parquet) and VRT file (ghsl_{filename}.vrt) within a 'study_area' subdirectory. The workflow is executed asynchronously via QgsTask and includes caching, existing file handling, and progress reporting.

task_name: Generate radial points from input points
task_description: The script generates radial point features in eight directions (N, S, E, O, NE, NO, SE, SO) from each input point feature. It supports three limiting modes: maximum distance (m), circular buffer radius (m), or fixed number of points per direction. For each direction, it iteratively places points at regular intervals (user-defined distance in meters), adjusting diagonal offsets by √2 to maintain Euclidean spacing. Output features include original feature ID, direction label, and cumulative distance (m), written to a new point vector layer with matching CRS.

The script performs spatial segmentation of a user-selected Area of Interest (AOI) vector layer into regular grid cells aligned to standardized cartographic map tile scales (e.g., 1:25k, 1:50k, etc.) or equal-sized rows/columns. It supports two modes: 'map_tile' (grid aligned to extent or geographic minute/degree snapping with configurable offsets and scale presets) and 'equal' (user-specified row/column count). Key operations include bounding box extraction, coordinate transformation (projected ↔ WGS84), dynamic tile width derivation in meters/km/arcminutes, offset application in map units or degrees, AOI intersection with grid cells, geometry validation, and output as segmented vector layers (Shapefiles) with metadata (row/col IDs, origin, scale, alignment). Outputs include preview layers in QGIS and persisted segmented Shapefiles organized in directory hierarchies under 'Base/Base Grid/[AOI name]/Segments'. No remote sensing data, time-series, or classification is performed — the input is purely vector-based AOI geometry; no satellite imagery or raster processing occurs.

The script splits input polygon parcels using three configurable methods: 'By measures' (grids defined by width and length), 'Equal parts' (geometric subdivision into N equal-area lots), or 'By area' (subdivision targeting a specified lot area). It uses Shapely for geometric operations including intersection, splitting, union, and small-area annexation based on boundary adjacency. Input parameters include width, length, number of parts, target area, and minimum area ratio for merging undersized lots. Outputs are polygon features with attributes 'split_id' and 'area', projected in the source CRS.

The script generalizes polygon and multipolygon features in a QGIS vector layer using the Douglas-Peucker algorithm (via QgsGeometry.simplify()) with a user-specified tolerance in map units. It supports two output modes: (1) creating a new temporary or permanent memory-based layer containing simplified geometries while preserving original attributes, or (2) in-place editing of the source layer’s geometries. Vertex counts before/after simplification are computed and reported, and history is recorded for undo support via base64-encoded WKB geometry backups. The action respects feature selection, handles edit mode automatically, and includes rollback-on-error and auto-commit capabilities.

The script computes distances between input and target point layers, supporting three output matrix types: linear (N*k x 3) with InputID, TargetID, and Distance; standard (N x T) with one row per input point and columns for each target point's distance; and summary (mean, std. dev., min, max) per input point. It uses QgsSpatialIndex for efficient nearest-neighbor search, QgsDistanceArea for geodetic distance measurement respecting CRS and ellipsoid, and validates input layers are single-point (not MultiPoint). Outputs are vector features with geometry and attribute fields as defined per matrix type.

The script generates legally compliant, orthogonally reoriented polygon geometries for mineral exploration applications in Brazil, adhering to ANM (Agência Nacional de Mineração) regulations. It accepts input polygons from QGIS project layers, user-drawn sketches on the map canvas, or external shapefiles; applies geodesic orthogonalization (ensuring strict N-S and E-W segment alignment per Portaria DNPM 155/2016); optionally clips against user-selected restriction layers (e.g., protected areas, infrastructure); validates orthogonality; computes geodesic area in hectares; converts coordinates to DMS format; and exports outputs as: (1) a shapefile (.shp) with metadata (e.g., observation notes), (2) an ANM-formatted TXT file listing vertices in DMS with header option, and (3) a CSV file formatted for REPEM batch import. All processing uses EPSG:4674 (SIRGAS 2000 Geographic), and results are visualized in QGIS with highlighting and logged with vertex coordinates and validation status. The study area is implicitly Brazil (via CRS:4674, ANM regulatory context, and CREA-DF licensing).

task_name: Classify land cover intervals by super-object ID
task_description: The script processes vector layers to group features into user-specified intervals based on a numeric attribute (e.g., 'diff_mean'), computes local reference values per super-object ID using the interval with the largest total area (summed from an 'Area' field), and calculates the difference between each feature's attribute value and its super-object’s local reference. Outputs include a vector layer with new fields: 'interval' (integer interval assignment), 'local_ref' (mean value of the dominant-area interval), and 'dif_to_ref' (difference from local reference). Input validation includes fallback to a backup layer if the primary layer is invalid or empty.

The script loads an ICNF burned area shapefile (or other reference shapefile) into QGIS, applies categorized symbology by month using a date field (configured via DATA0), labels features by day of month, sets the project CRS to match the layer, and zooms the map canvas to the layer extent. Optionally, it merges and loads CCD vectorized results from GeoPackage files for visual comparison, applying distinct symbology and labeling. The output is a QGIS project with two layers (reference burned area and optional CCD vector results), each styled with month-based color categories and day-based labels.

task_name: Copy and clip vector feature class
task_description: The script copies a source vector layer (e.g., from a shapefile or GeoPackage) to a new GeoPackage file at a specified output path. If a mask tuple is provided, it clips the source features to the geometry of a filtered 'sample_frame_features' layer (filtered by 'sample_frame_id'), performing coordinate transformation and intersection-based clipping. The output is a GeoPackage layer containing either the full source layer or its spatially clipped subset. No raster data, time-series analysis, classification, or satellite-derived products are involved — this is purely a vector I/O and geometric clipping operation within QGIS using GDAL/OGR-backed QgsVectorFileWriter and QgsVectorLayer APIs.
